lessons.title: Hash partitioning and in-memory join I/O
lessons.summary: Hash partitioning and in-memory join I/O using explicit models and assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plans and figures below are illustrative model inputs. Actual execution depends on version, workload and settings.

This unit uses R occupying 1,000 pages, S occupying 500 pages and a budget of 102 buffer pages. CPU work, partition slack and final output writes are excluded.

### Grace hash

Partition both tables by hashing the join key into one fewer partition than the available buffer pages, writing the partitions to disk. Matching rows always land in partitions with the same number, so each pair of partitions is then joined on its own in memory:

```formula
C_GH = 2 × (M + N) + (M + N)
C_GH = 3 × (1,000 + 500)
C_GH = 4,500
where
C_GH: the cost of a Grace hash join, in page I/Os
M: the number of pages in R, here 1,000
N: the number of pages in S, here 500
In words: partitioning reads and writes both tables (2 I/Os per page), then joining the partition pairs reads them once more (1 I/O per page).
```

This needs each partition of the smaller table to fit in memory. Here S's 500 pages split into 101 partitions of about 5 pages, which fit easily. If the hash spreads keys badly, some partitions are too big and must be partitioned again.

### Hash, when S fits in memory

The current 500-page S does not fit the 102-page fixture; this next case instead assumes a larger memory budget sufficient for S and hash overhead.

If all of S fits in memory, build the hash table from S and stream R past it: each table is read once, 1,000 + 500 = 1,500 page I/Os. This is the full-input scan lower bound for this unindexed model. It does not apply to joins that can skip data using indexes or other knowledge.

## Key takeaways
- Grace hash reads and writes partitions, then reads them for joining; the simple model excludes skew and output writes.
- The single-read in-memory case needs enough space for the build table and hash overhead.

## Further reading
- [Hash join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_join)
- [Sort-merge join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sort-merge_join)
- [Nested loop join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nested_loop_join)
- [Planner/optimiser: join strategies — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-optimizer.html)
- [Resource consumption: work_mem and hash_mem_multiplier — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html)

questions.prompt: Same tables: R has 2,000 pages and S has 400 pages. Neither fits in memory, but there is enough memory for a two-phase Grace hash join. What does it cost in page I/Os?

options.explanation: That reads each input once: reading each table once. It only applies when the build side fits entirely in memory, which the question rules out.
That is twice the combined page count, the partitioning phase alone. The partitions must then be read again to join them.
That is five times the combined page count, the cost of a sort-merge join that writes each sorted table out before merging.
Correct. Partition both tables by hash of the key (read and write each: 2 x 2,400), then read each partition pair once to join (2,400): 3 x 2,400.

questions.workedExample:
Grace hash join has two phases. Partitioning reads both tables and writes them back out as partitions (2 I/Os per page). Joining reads each pair of partitions once (1 I/O per page):

```formula
C_GH = 2 × (M + N) + (M + N)
C_GH = 2 × 2,400 + 2,400
C_GH = 3 × 2,400 = 7,200
where
C_GH: the cost of a Grace hash join, in page I/Os (each page read or written counts as one)
M: the number of pages in R, 2,000
N: the number of pages in S, 400
In words: every page is read, written, then read again: 3 I/Os per page of the two tables.
```

Compare with the block nested loop's best of 16,400 from the previous question. The output write is excluded in both, as is conventional.

lessons.title: Index probe costs and cost crossovers
lessons.summary: Index probe costs and cost crossovers with explicit page-I/O assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Index nested-loop I/O

Use a 1,000-page outer table R with 100,000 rows and an indexed inner table S. This deliberately cold, simplified page-I/O model excludes CPU and final output writes.

### Index nested loop

> [!note] What about index nested loop?
> Instead of scanning S for each outer row, probe an index on S's join column. With a 3-level B-tree plus a heap page, that's about 4 random reads per outer row.

```formula
C_INL = M + |R| × c_probe
C_INL = 1,000 + 100,000 × 4
C_INL = 401,000
where
C_INL: the cost of an index nested loop join, in page I/Os
M: the number of pages in the outer table R, here 1,000
R: the outer table
|R|: the number of rows in R, here 100,000
c_probe: the page reads for one index lookup: 3 to walk down a 3-level B-tree, plus 1 for the heap page holding the row, so about 4
In words: one index lookup per outer row, so the cost grows with the number of outer rows, not the size of S.
```

For 100,000 outer rows that's about 400,000 random reads, far worse than hashing. For 100 outer rows it's about 400 probe reads, far better. Index nested loop wins when the outer side is small.

Why only 3 levels? Each B-tree page holds hundreds of keys, so every level multiplies the number of reachable entries by hundreds:

```formula
h = ⌈log_f(n)⌉
h = ⌈log_{300}(1,000,000)⌉
h = ⌈2.42⌉ = 3
where
h: an idealised number of page levels on a root-to-leaf path, assuming fanout and leaf capacity both equal f; real occupancy and page metadata change height
n: greater than one; the number of entries in the idealised index, here 1,000,000
f: a value greater than one for the assumed fanout, the number of child pointers per page; a few hundred for small keys in 8 KiB pages, 300 here as an illustration
log_f: the logarithm to base f: how many times you must divide by f to get down to 1
log_{300}: the logarithm to base 300; log_300(1,000,000) ≈ 2.42, because 300 × 300 = 90,000 is too few and 300 × 300 × 300 = 27,000,000 is more than enough
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to the next whole number
In words: a tree whose pages each point to about 300 others reaches a million entries in 3 levels, and 27 million in the same 3.
```

The upper levels are read on almost every lookup, so they are usually already in memory, and a real probe often needs fewer than four disk reads.

## Key takeaways
- A cold index probe pays for B-tree traversal and heap access; cached tree levels can reduce physical reads.
- Compare the probe model with hashing using the actual outer row count and workload-specific costs.

## Further reading
- [Hash join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_join)
- [Sort-merge join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sort-merge_join)
- [Nested loop join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nested_loop_join)
- [Planner/optimiser: join strategies — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-optimizer.html)
- [Resource consumption: work_mem and hash_mem_multiplier — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html)

questions.prompt: A toy model: an index nested loop costs 4 random page reads per outer row, at 4 units each. A hash join costs one sequential scan of the 1,029-page inner table at 1 unit per page (ignore CPU). Roughly how many outer rows make the two plans cost the same?

options.text: About 64
options.explanation: Correct. Each outer row costs 4 x 4 = 16 units in the nested loop. 1,029 / 16 is about 64 rows.

options.text: About 257
options.explanation: That's 1,029 / 4: it charges 4 pages per row but forgets that random pages cost 4 units each.

options.text: About 1,029
options.explanation: That assumes one unit per outer row. Each probe touches several pages, and random reads are charged more.

options.text: There is no crossover; the nested loop is always cheaper with an index
options.explanation: The nested loop's cost grows linearly with outer rows while the scan's cost is fixed, so there's always a crossover.

questions.workedExample:
Set the two costs equal and solve for the number of outer rows:

```formula
C_NL = k × p × c_rand
C_hash = P × c_seq
k × 4 × 4 = 1,029 × 1
k = 1,029 / 16 ≈ 64
where
C_NL: the cost of the index nested loop, in planner cost units
C_hash: the cost of the hash join's single scan of the inner table, in planner cost units
k: the number of outer rows
p: the random page reads per outer row, here 4
c_rand: the cost of one random page read, here 4 units
P: the number of pages in the inner table, here 1,029
c_seq: the cost of one sequential page read, 1 unit
≈: approximately equal to
In words: each outer row costs the nested loop 16 units, so about 64 outer rows cost the same as one 1,029-page scan.
```

Below about 64 outer rows the index probes win; above, scanning the inner table once and hashing wins. Real planners add CPU costs, caching effects (`effective_cache_size`) and correlation, so the real crossover moves, but the shape is the same. That's why a misestimate of the outer row count flips the join choice.

lessons.title: Join choices and outer, semi and anti variants
lessons.summary: Join choices and outer, semi and anti variants using explicit models and assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plans and figures below are illustrative model inputs. Actual execution depends on version, workload and settings.

## Choosing between them

| | Nested loop | Hash | Merge |
|---|---|---|---|
| Join condition | Any | Equality | Equality |
| Best when | Small outer, indexed inner | Large unsorted inputs | Inputs already sorted |
| Memory | Little | Build side | Little (if presorted) |
| Internal path order | May preserve outer | None promised | May preserve merge keys |

The illustrative plan costs show why an access path can matter. Joining pending orders to customers:

| Plan | Estimated cost |
|---|---|
| Hash join | 23,290 |
| Merge join | 25,539 |
| Nested loop + index | 30,572 |
| Nested loop, no index | 46,172,536 |

Without an index on the inner side, the nested loop is about 2,000 times more expensive. That's the plan you get when an index is missing **and** no equality condition exists, or when the planner wrongly believes the outer side has one row.

At larger scale, joining all 1,000,000 orders to their 3,000,000 order items, the hash join (8 batches, 587 ms) beat a merge join that had to sort 3 million rows through a 35 MB temporary file (850 ms).

A physical path may provide useful ordering to another node, but SQL results have a guaranteed order only with ORDER BY. Outer joins and duplicate groups can limit which path ordering is useful.

## Outer, semi and anti joins

All three algorithms come in variants for other join types, and you'll see the names in plans:

- `Hash Left Join`, `Merge Full Join`: outer joins. Postgres can't run a `FULL OUTER JOIN` as a nested loop, because the nested loop has no cheap way to remember which inner rows never matched.
- `Semi Join`: from `EXISTS` or `IN`. Stops at the first matching row for each outer row.
- `Anti Join`: from `NOT EXISTS`. Emits outer rows with no match.
- `Hash Right Join`: the planner swapped sides so the smaller input is hashed, even though the SQL said `LEFT JOIN`.

## Key takeaways
- Join cost depends on outer cardinality, input ordering, memory and usable access paths.
- Join variants preserve different rows; input swaps can change the displayed direction, and only ORDER BY promises result order.

## Further reading
- [Hash join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_join)
- [Sort-merge join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sort-merge_join)
- [Nested loop join — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nested_loop_join)
- [Planner/optimiser: join strategies — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-optimizer.html)
- [Resource consumption: work_mem and hash_mem_multiplier — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html)

questions.prompt: Which statements about join variants in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A general equijoin `FULL OUTER JOIN` can use hash or merge join; PostgreSQL does not implement a general full nested-loop join
options.explanation: Correct. A full join must also emit inner rows that never matched. Hash and merge joins can track that; Postgres's nested loop can't, so full joins need a hash- or merge-joinable condition.

options.text: `WHERE EXISTS (subquery)` is typically planned as a Semi Join, which stops at the first matching row for each outer row
options.explanation: Correct. A semi join never returns an outer row twice, so it can stop probing after the first matching row.

options.text: A `Hash Right Join` in the plan means the SQL must have said `RIGHT JOIN`
options.explanation: No. The planner may swap the inputs of a LEFT JOIN so the smaller one is hashed, and it then appears as a Hash Right Join.

options.text: `NOT EXISTS (subquery)` can be planned as an Anti Join
options.explanation: Correct. An anti join emits outer rows that have no match, which is exactly NOT EXISTS.

options.text: Merge join cannot provide useful join-key ordering to a parent node
options.explanation: A compatible inner merge join can provide useful merge-key ordering and avoid a later sort. Outer joins and path details can limit the usable ordering, and only SQL ORDER BY guarantees result order.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each:

1. FULL JOIN needs to remember unmatched inner rows. Hash join marks matched entries in its table; merge join sees them as it walks. True.
2. EXISTS: one match is enough, so Semi Join. True.
3. Hash Right Join: the side swap is the planner's choice. False.
4. NOT EXISTS: Anti Join (Postgres 16+ can even show `Hash Right Anti Join`). True.
5. Claiming merge joins cannot provide useful ordering is false. Check the join type and path order before relying on it; ORDER BY supplies the SQL guarantee.

lessons.title: What column statistics record
lessons.summary: Reading sampled column distributions, statistics targets and physical-order correlation.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

The optimiser has to choose between plans without running them. It does this by **predicting** how many rows each step will produce, converting those predictions into a cost, and picking the cheapest plan it can find. This design, the **cost-based optimiser**, comes from IBM's System R in the late 1970s (Selinger et al., 1979), and remains influential in modern query optimisers.

An optimiser has three parts:

1. **Cardinality estimation**: how many rows will each operator produce?
2. **A cost model**: given those row counts, how expensive is each operator?
3. **A search strategy**: which of the possible plans does it actually consider?

Cardinality estimation is a major source of poor choices. Leis et al., *How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?* (VLDB 2015), found large estimation errors on its evaluated join workloads; that evidence does not establish one cause for every slow query.

## What the planner knows

`ANALYZE` (run manually or by autovacuum) reads a random sample of each table and stores a summary. Table-level figures live in `pg_class`; column-level ones are in the `pg_stats` view.

```sql
-- Inspect sampled column distributions.
SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct,
       most_common_vals,
       most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders';
```

For our `orders` table:

| Column | Statistic | Value |
|---|---|---|
| status | n_distinct | 3 |
| status | most common values | shipped, cancelled, pending |
| status | their frequencies | 0.8976, 0.0716, 0.0308 |
| customer_id | n_distinct | 91,709 |
| ordered_on | histogram | 101 bounds |

- **null_frac**: the fraction of NULLs.
- **n_distinct**: the number of distinct values. A negative number means a fraction of the row count (-1 means "every row is unique", as for a primary key).
- **most_common_vals / most_common_freqs (MCVs)**: the most frequent values and how often each appears.
- **histogram_bounds**: values that split the *remaining* (non-MCV) rows into buckets holding equal numbers of rows.
- **physical-order correlation**: how closely the physical row order follows the column's sort order, from -1 to 1. It affects how expensive an index scan's heap reads will be.

For PostgreSQL 18's built-in scalar statistics analysis, the target sample size uses the following model. Special data-type analysers and other requested statistics can affect the required sample:

```formula
n_sample = 300 × t_stats
n_sample = 300 × 100
n_sample = 30,000
where
n_sample: the target sample row count for the standard scalar analyser on a sufficiently large table; the available rows and analyser requirements can change the actual sample
t_stats: the statistics target: `default_statistics_target` (default 100), or a per-column value set with `SET STATISTICS`; the largest target among the table's columns is used
300: a multiplier fixed in PostgreSQL's source code, chosen from a statistical result (Chaudhuri, Motwani and Narasayya, 1998) on how large a random sample must be to build a reliable histogram
In words: with target 100, the standard scalar analyser requests 30,000 sample rows from a sufficiently large table; this is not a universal rule for every type or table.
```

With that default the standard scalar-statistics analyser can retain up to 100 MCVs and about 100 histogram buckets per column. Raising a column's target to 1,000 samples 300,000 rows and keeps up to 1,000 of each, at the cost of a slower ANALYZE and slightly slower planning.

> [!note] The estimates are estimates
> Because ANALYZE samples, the numbers change slightly each time it runs. That's why the planner said 30,767 pending orders when the true count is 30,066.

## Key takeaways
- ANALYZE collects sampled column distributions; the scalar-statistics target controls detail and the requested sample.
- Physical-order correlation concerns heap ordering, whereas inter-column dependence requires multivariate statistics.

## Further reading
- [Statistics used by the planner — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-stats.html)
- [Row estimation examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/row-estimation-examples.html)
- [Multivariate statistics examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/multivariate-statistics-examples.html)
- [Access path selection in a relational DBMS (Selinger et al., 1979)](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/compsci516/cps216/spring03/papers/selinger-etal-1979.pdf)
- [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (Leis et al., VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf)
- [Genetic query optimiser — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/geqo.html)

questions.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL's `pg_stats` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: `n_distinct = -1` means every row has a different value
options.explanation: Correct. Negative values are a fraction of the row count, so -1 means distinct values = rows, as for a primary key. It scales automatically as the table grows.

options.text: The histogram covers the values not in the most-common-values list
options.explanation: Correct. MCVs are handled exactly by frequency; the histogram describes the rest, split into buckets with equal numbers of rows.

options.text: Statistics are updated on every INSERT
options.explanation: They're only updated by ANALYZE (manual or autovacuum). That's why bulk loads can leave stats stale.

options.text: `correlation` near 1 means the table's physical order matches the column's order, making index range scans cheaper
options.explanation: Correct. Rows that are adjacent in the index are then adjacent on disk, so a range scan reads few heap pages. Near 0, each index entry may point to a different page.

options.text: ANALYZE reads every row of the table
options.explanation: For large tables it uses a sample; the target depends on column types and statistics targets. Small tables can be read completely.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each:

1. `n_distinct`: a positive number is a distinct-value count; a negative number represents a fraction of rows. `orders.id` shows -1. True.
2. MCV list plus histogram partition the values. True.
3. Stats come only from ANALYZE. False.
4. Correlation: `orders.id` has 1.0 because ids were inserted in order. True.
5. The claim that ANALYZE always reads every row is false. Standard scalar analysis requests about 30,000 sample rows at target 100 on sufficiently large tables; other types and smaller tables differ.

lessons.title: Equality selectivity from column statistics
lessons.summary: Equality selectivity from column statistics using explicit models and assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plans and figures below are illustrative model inputs. Actual execution depends on version, workload and settings.

## Selectivity: from stats to row counts

**Selectivity** is the fraction of rows a condition keeps. Every row estimate starts from it:

```formula
n_est = s × n_table
where
n_est: the planner's estimated number of rows the condition keeps (its cardinality estimate)
s: the selectivity of the condition: the fraction of rows it keeps, from 0 (none) to 1 (all)
n_table: the planner's estimate of the number of rows in the table, from `pg_class.reltuples` scaled to the table's current size
In words: the estimated row count is the fraction of rows the condition keeps, times the number of rows in the table.
```

The rules below are all ways of working out *s*, using the illustrative column-frequency statistics.

### Equality on a common value

`WHERE status = 'pending'`: 'pending' is in the MCV list, so the planner uses its measured frequency, 0.030767, as the selectivity:

```formula
n_est = f_MCV × n_table
n_est = 0.030767 × 1,000,000
n_est = 30,767
where
n_est: the estimated number of matching rows
f_MCV: the value's frequency in the most-common-values (MCV) list: the fraction of sampled rows holding it, here 0.030767 for 'pending'
n_table: the number of rows in the table, here 1,000,000
In words: if about 3.1% of the sample was 'pending', expect about 3.1% of the table to be.
```

The actual count is 30,066, so the estimate is about 2% high.

### Equality on any other value

`WHERE customer_id = 42`: there's no MCV list (no value is especially common), so the planner assumes values are evenly spread and every value matches the same share of rows. The column has no NULLs here; if it had, their fraction would be taken off first:

```formula
s = 1 / n_distinct
n_est = n_table / n_distinct
n_est = 1,000,000 / 91,709
n_est ≈ 10.9 ≈ 11
where
s: the selectivity: the fraction of rows expected to match
n_distinct: the estimated number of distinct values in the column, here 91,709 customer ids
n_est: the estimated number of matching rows, rounded to a whole number
n_table: the number of rows in the table, here 1,000,000
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a million orders shared evenly among about 92,000 customers gives about 11 orders per customer.
```

The actual count for customer 42 is 14: close enough to choose the right plan.

This residual model requires a positive count of remaining distinct non-NULL values.

When the column *does* have an MCV list but the value isn't on it, the planner takes away the rows the MCVs and NULLs account for and shares the rest evenly among the remaining distinct values:

```formula
s = (1 − Σ f_MCV − f_null)
    / (n_distinct − n_MCV)
where
s: the selectivity for a value not in the MCV list
Σ f_MCV: the sum of the frequencies of all the values in the MCV list
Σ: sum: add up the terms
f_MCV: the frequency of one most-common value
f_null: the fraction of rows that are NULL (`null_frac`)
n_distinct: the estimated number of distinct values in the column
n_MCV: the number of values in the MCV list
In words: whatever fraction of rows isn't covered by the common values or NULLs is assumed to be spread evenly over the values that aren't common.
```

For example, if 3 MCVs cover 40% of rows, there are no NULLs and 103 distinct values, the remaining 60% of rows are shared among 100 values, giving 0.6% per value. PostgreSQL also caps this figure so that a value missing from the list is never estimated as more common than the least common value on it.

## Key takeaways
- Use MCV frequencies for listed values; share residual probability among the remaining distinct non-NULL values.
- The estimates assume sampled frequencies and distinct counts represent the current table.

## Further reading
- [Statistics used by the planner — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-stats.html)
- [Row estimation examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/row-estimation-examples.html)
- [Multivariate statistics examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/multivariate-statistics-examples.html)
- [Access path selection in a relational DBMS (Selinger et al., 1979)](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/compsci516/cps216/spring03/papers/selinger-etal-1979.pdf)
- [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (Leis et al., VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf)
- [Genetic query optimiser — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/geqo.html)

questions.prompt:
`pg_stats` for `orders.status` (1,000,000 rows) shows:

```

  {shipped,cancelled,pending}
most_common_freqs:
  {0.8976,0.0716,0.0308}
```

How many rows will the planner estimate for `WHERE status = 'cancelled'`?

options.explanation: That's 1/3, treating the three values as equally common. The MCV list exists precisely so the planner doesn't have to assume that.
Correct. 'cancelled' is in the MCV list, so the planner uses its measured frequency: 0.0716 x 1,000,000.
That's the 0.5% default for equality when there are no usable statistics. Here there are.
A 1-row estimate happens when a value appears to be absent from the sample. 'cancelled' is clearly present.

1. Is the value in `most_common_vals`? Yes, in position 2.
2. Take the matching frequency: 0.0716.
3. Multiply by the table's row count:

where

In words: 7.16% of the sampled rows were 'cancelled', so the planner expects 7.16% of the table to be.
```

The illustrative estimate is `rows=71600`. ANALYZE samples large tables (typically about 30,000 rows with the default target for built-in scalar types), so sampled frequency need not equal the true frequency.

questions.prompt: For `orders.customer_id`, `pg_stats` shows `n_distinct = 91709` and no most-common values. The table has 1,000,000 rows and no NULL customer IDs. What does the planner estimate for `WHERE customer_id = 42`?

options.text: About 91,709
options.explanation: That's the number of distinct values, not the rows per value. It inverts the calculation.

options.text: Exactly 14, the real count
options.explanation: The planner doesn't count rows at plan time; that would require running the query. It estimates from statistics.

options.text: About 11
options.explanation: Correct. With no MCVs, it assumes the rows are spread evenly over the distinct values: 1,000,000 / 91,709 = 10.9, rounded to 11.

options.text: About 5,000
options.explanation: That's the 0.5% default for an expression with no statistics. A plain column with stats gets a proper estimate.

s = 1 / 91,709
n_est = n_table × s
n_est = 1,000,000 / 91,709
n_est ≈ 10.9 ≈ 11
where
s: the selectivity: the fraction of rows expected to match
n_distinct: the estimated number of distinct values in the column, 91,709
n_est: the estimated number of matching rows, rounded to a whole number
n_table: the number of rows in the table, 1,000,000
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a million rows shared evenly among about 92,000 values gives about 11 rows per value.
```

(If there were MCVs, the planner would first subtract their total frequency and divide the rest among the remaining distinct values.) The real count for customer 42 is 14, so the estimate is close. Good enough to pick an index scan.

lessons.title: Ranges and dependent filters
lessons.summary: Ranges and dependent filters with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Range selectivity and dependencies

Selectivity is the fraction of input rows retained by a condition; cardinality is the number retained. The numerical statistics below are illustrative, rather than measurements of the small executable fixtures.

### A range, from the histogram

`WHERE ordered_on >= '2026-01-01'`: the histogram has 100 buckets, each holding 1% of the non-MCV rows. The date leaves one third of the bucket above it; that bucket runs from 2025-12-18 to 2026-01-08, and 8 more buckets lie above it. Count the buckets above the constant, including the part of the bucket it falls in:

```formula
s_hist ≈ (b_full + b_part) / b_total
s_hist ≈ (8 + 1/3) / 100
s_hist ≈ 0.083 (8.3%)
where
s_hist: the fraction of the histogram's rows that satisfy the condition
b_full: the number of complete buckets lying entirely above the constant, here 8
b_part: the fraction of the constant's own bucket that lies above it, here 1/3, found by assuming values are spread evenly across the bucket (linear interpolation)
b_total: the number of buckets in the histogram, here 100
≈: approximately equal to
In words: about 8⅓ of the 100 equal-sized buckets lie above 1 January, so about 8.3% of the rows do.
```

The planner applies that fraction to the non-MCV rows and adds the frequencies of any MCVs that satisfy the condition, which is why its final estimate, 84,278 rows, is slightly above 8.3%. The actual count is 86,346.

### Combining conditions: the independence assumption

For conditions A and B, PostgreSQL normally multiplies their selectivities when it has no applicable dependency information, assuming the columns are **independent**: knowing a row's value in one column tells you nothing about the other. For `status = 'pending' AND ordered_on >= '2026-01-01'`:

```formula
s_AND = s_A × s_B
n_est = s_A × s_B × n_table
n_est = 0.030767 × 0.084278 × 1,000,000
n_est ≈ 2,593
where
s_AND: the selectivity of the combined condition A AND B
s_A: the selectivity of the first condition, here 0.030767 for status = 'pending'
s_B: the selectivity of the second condition, here 0.084278 for the date range (84,278 of 1,000,000 rows)
n_est: the estimated number of rows satisfying both conditions
n_table: the number of rows in the table, here 1,000,000
≈: approximately equal to
In words: if 3% of orders are pending and 8.4% are recent, and the two are unrelated, about 3% of the recent orders are pending: about 2,600 rows.
```

The illustrative calculation assumes status and date are independent; that assumption needs checking on real data. But consider `customers`, where every Glasgow customer is in Scotland:

```sql
-- Both filters describe the same group.
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Glasgow'
  AND country = 'Scotland';
```

The eight cities are equally common; Glasgow and Scotland each cover 1/8 of customers in this fixture, so the planner multiplies:

```formula
n_est = s_city × s_country × n_table
n_est = 1/8 × 1/8 × 100,000
n_est ≈ 1,560
where
n_est: the planner's estimated number of matching customers
s_city: the selectivity of city = 'Glasgow', 1/8
s_country: the selectivity of country = 'Scotland', 1/8
n_table: the number of customers, 100,000
≈: approximately equal to (the exact product is 1,562.5)
In words: treating city and country as unrelated, the planner expects one eighth of one eighth of the customers.
```

The actual count is 12,500, one eighth of the customers. The planner is out by a factor of 8 because knowing the city already tells you the country. Errors like this can affect plan choices for multi-column filters.

### Extended statistics

You can tell Postgres to measure the relationship:

```sql
-- Measure dependence before replanning.
CREATE STATISTICS cust_city_country
  (dependencies) ON city, country
  FROM customers;
ANALYZE customers;
```

ANALYZE then records that `city` determines `country` with degree 1.0, and the estimate becomes about 12,700. Other kinds are `ndistinct` (for `GROUP BY a, b` estimates) and `mcv` (common *combinations* of values).

## Key takeaways
- Histograms describe non-MCV rows and interpolate within buckets.
- Multiplying selectivities assumes independence; suitable extended statistics can measure dependencies or value combinations.

questions.prompt: A 2,000,000-row `events` table has `region = 'eu'` with selectivity 0.2 and `kind = 'click'` with selectivity 0.05. The two columns are unrelated. What does Postgres estimate for `WHERE region = 'eu' AND kind = 'click'`?

options.explanation: Correct. Under the independence assumption the planner multiplies selectivities: 0.2 x 0.05 = 0.01, and 0.01 x 2,000,000 = 20,000.
That uses only the more selective condition (0.05 x 2,000,000). AND keeps rows satisfying both, so it's smaller.
That adds the selectivities (0.25). Adding is roughly what you'd do for OR, not AND.
That uses only the region condition. The kind condition removes most of those rows too.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
s_AND = s_A × s_B
s_AND = 0.2 × 0.05 = 0.01
n_est = s_AND × n_table
n_est = 0.01 × 2,000,000 = 20,000
where
s_AND: the selectivity of the combined condition A AND B
s_A: the selectivity of region = 'eu', 0.2
s_B: the selectivity of kind = 'click', 0.05
n_est: the estimated number of rows matching both
n_table: the number of rows in the table, 2,000,000
In words: if a fifth of events are EU and a twentieth are clicks, and the two are unrelated, a hundredth of events are EU clicks.
```

This is exactly right if the columns are independent. If they aren't independent (say every click comes from the EU), the true answer is 100,000 and the estimate is five times too low. Applicable multivariate MCV statistics can improve this estimate; functional dependencies help only when their assumptions match the relationship. One-way implication does not establish a full functional dependency. For OR, Postgres adds the two selectivities and subtracts the overlap, which would otherwise be counted twice:

```formula
s_OR = s_A + s_B − s_A × s_B
s_OR = 0.2 + 0.05 − 0.01 = 0.24
where
s_OR: the selectivity of A OR B
s_A: the selectivity of region = 'eu', 0.2
s_B: the selectivity of kind = 'click', 0.05
In words: rows matching either condition, minus the EU clicks that both conditions already counted.
```

questions.prompt: In `customers` (100,000 rows), 8 cities are equally common, and `country` is always determined by `city`; Glasgow and Scotland each occur in 1/8 of rows. EXPLAIN for `WHERE city = 'Glasgow' AND country = 'Scotland'` says `rows=1559`; the true answer is 12,500. What's the best fix?

options.text: Raise `default_statistics_target` to 1000 and re-analyse
options.explanation: A bigger sample makes each column's frequencies slightly more precise, but the planner still multiplies them as if independent. The 8x error remains.

options.text: Add an index on `(city, country)`
options.explanation: A plain multi-column index doesn't give the planner combined selectivity statistics. The estimate would stay around 1,560.

options.text: Create extended statistics on the two columns and re-analyse
options.explanation: Correct. `CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies) ON city, country` records that city determines country (degree 1.0), and the estimate rises to about 12,700.

options.text: Nothing; Postgres can't estimate correlated columns
options.explanation: It can since Postgres 10, via extended statistics. It just doesn't by default.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each condition alone: about 1/8 of rows (frequency about 0.125).
2. Independence: the planner multiplies the two fractions.
3. Reality: every Glasgow row is Scottish, so the country condition removes nothing extra.

```formula
n_est = s_city × s_country × n_table
n_est = 0.125 × 0.125 × 100,000 ≈ 1,560
n_act = s_city × n_table
n_act = 0.125 × 100,000 = 12,500
where
n_est: the planner's estimate, assuming the columns are independent
n_act: the true count
s_city: the fraction of customers in Glasgow, 0.125 (1/8)
s_country: the fraction of customers in Scotland, 0.125 (1/8)
n_table: the number of customers, 100,000
≈: approximately equal to
In words: multiplying counts the Scotland condition again although Glasgow already implies it, so the estimate is 8 times too low.
```

```sql
CREATE STATISTICS cust_city_country
  (dependencies) ON city, country
  FROM customers;
ANALYZE customers;
```

ANALYZE then records `city => country: 1.0`, and the planner stops double-counting the restriction.

questions.prompt: A column has no MCVs, so its histogram describes all 2,000,000 rows in 100 equal-count buckets. The constant `v` lies 25% of the way through bucket 41 (40 complete buckets lie below it). Assuming linear interpolation within the bucket, what is the estimate for `WHERE col < v`?

options.explanation: That counts all of bucket 41 as below `v` (41%). Only the first quarter of that bucket lies below.
Correct. 40 full buckets plus a quarter of bucket 41 is 40.25% of the rows: 0.4025 x 2,000,000.
That's the estimate for `col >= v` (59.75%). The question asks for rows below `v`.
That's the 1/3 default for inequalities without statistics. Here a histogram exists, so it's used.

questions.workedExample:
Each bucket holds 1% of the rows (20,000 rows).

```formula
s ≈ (b_full + b_part) / b_total
s ≈ (40 + 0.25) / 100 = 0.4025
n_est = s × n_table
n_est = 0.4025 × 2,000,000 = 805,000
where
s: the selectivity: the fraction of rows below the query constant
b_full: the complete buckets lying entirely below the query constant, 40
b_part: the fraction of bucket 41 lying below the query constant, 0.25
b_total: the number of buckets, 100
n_est: the estimated number of matching rows
n_table: the number of rows the histogram describes, 2,000,000
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 40 and a quarter of the 100 equal buckets lie below the query constant, so about 40.25% of the rows do.
```

The lesson's date example worked the same way from the other end: 8 full buckets above plus a third of one gave about 8.3%.

lessons.title: Unknown expressions, joins and scan costs
lessons.summary: Unknown expressions, joins and scan costs with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Missing expression statistics and join estimates

The worked estimates use an illustrative million-row orders table and 100,000 customers; IDs are non-NULL and each order references exactly one customer.

### When there are no statistics

For conditions the planner can't analyse, it uses fixed default selectivities:

| Condition | Default | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `expr = const` | 0.5% | `lower(email) = '...'`: 500 of 100,000 |
| `expr < const` | 1/3 | `price * 2 > 100`: 3,333 of 10,000 |

The planner has stats on the `email` column, but not on `lower(email)`. An **expression index** on `lower(email)` allows expression statistics as a side effect, because ANALYZE then gathers statistics on the indexed expression.

### Join estimates

For an equijoin (a join on `=`), the selectivity is the fraction of all possible row pairs that match. Postgres estimates it from the distinct counts of the two join keys, refined using MCV lists where it has them. For `orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id`:

```formula
s_join ≈ 1 / max(d_R, d_S)
n_est = n_R × n_S × s_join
n_est = 1,000,000 × 100,000 / 100,000
n_est = 1,000,000
where
s_join: the join selectivity: the fraction of all (order, customer) pairs that satisfy the join condition
max: the larger of the values in brackets
d_R: the number of distinct values of the join key in orders, here 91,709 customer ids
d_S: the number of distinct values of the join key in customers, here 100,000 ids
n_R: the number of rows in orders, 1,000,000
n_S: the number of rows in customers, 100,000
n_est: the estimated number of rows the join produces
≈: approximately equal to
In words: every order matches one customer out of 100,000, so the join produces one row per order: about a million.
```

The formula assumes every key value on the side with fewer distinct values has a match on the other side, which is exactly true for a foreign key.

Errors **multiply** as they go up the tree. If each of three joins is out by a factor of 3, the final estimate can be out by 27, and the join algorithm choices near the top are made on wrong numbers.

## The cost model

Postgres costs are in arbitrary units anchored on one sequential page read = 1.0:

| Parameter | Default | Charged for |
|---|---|---|
| `seq_page_cost` | 1.0 | Page read in order |
| `random_page_cost` | 4.0 | Page read at random |
| `cpu_tuple_cost` | 0.01 | Each row processed |
| `cpu_index_tuple_cost` | 0.005 | Each index entry |
| `cpu_operator_cost` | 0.0025 | Each operator or function call |

A sequential scan pays for every page it reads, every row it processes and every condition it evaluates on each row. For `orders` with `status = 'pending'`:

```formula
C_seq = P × c_page
      + n × c_tuple
      + n × q × c_op
C_seq = 7,353 × 1.0
      + 1,000,000 × 0.01
      + 1,000,000 × 1 × 0.0025
C_seq = 7,353 + 10,000 + 2,500
C_seq = 19,853
where
C_seq: the estimated total cost of the sequential scan, in planner cost units (1 unit = one sequential page read)
P: the number of pages in the table, here 7,353
c_page: `seq_page_cost`, default 1.0 per page read in order
n: the number of rows in the table, here 1,000,000
c_tuple: `cpu_tuple_cost`, default 0.01 per row processed
q: the number of operators (comparisons) in the filter evaluated on each row, here 1 for status = 'pending'
c_op: `cpu_operator_cost`, default 0.0025 per operator or function call
In words: read 7,353 pages, process a million rows and test one condition on each; the row work costs more than the page reads.
```

EXPLAIN shows `cost=0.00..19853.00`: exactly this. An index scan's cost depends on how many index and heap pages it expects to touch, charged at `random_page_cost`, discounted by physical-order correlation and `effective_cache_size` (the planner's guess of how much data is cached).

> [!tip] Tune random_page_cost for SSDs
> The default of 4.0 dates from spinning disks. On SSDs, or when most data is cached, many teams set it to around 1.1 so the planner is less reluctant to use indexes. Test the change on your workload first.

## Key takeaways
- Missing expression statistics can trigger defaults; indexed expressions can collect statistics after ANALYZE.
- Planner costs combine page and CPU terms in relative cost units, rather than milliseconds.

## Further reading
- [Statistics used by the planner — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-stats.html)
- [Row estimation examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/row-estimation-examples.html)
- [Multivariate statistics examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/multivariate-statistics-examples.html)
- [Access path selection in a relational DBMS (Selinger et al., 1979)](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/compsci516/cps216/spring03/papers/selinger-etal-1979.pdf)
- [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (Leis et al., VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf)
- [Genetic query optimiser — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/geqo.html)

questions.prompt: A table has 5,000 pages and 400,000 rows. In the simplified nonparallel model with default costs, integer comparisons and no additional projection costs, what total cost does a Seq Scan have with **two** filter conditions (`WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2`)?

options.explanation: That's pages plus `cpu_tuple_cost` per row, but it forgets the `cpu_operator_cost` for evaluating the two conditions on each row.
That counts only one condition (400,000 x 0.0025 = 1,000). Each condition is charged separately.
That charges `random_page_cost` (4) for 5,000 pages. A sequential scan uses `seq_page_cost` (1).
Correct. 5,000 x 1.0 for pages, 400,000 x 0.01 for rows, and 400,000 x 2 x 0.0025 for the two comparisons: 5,000 + 4,000 + 2,000.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
C_seq = P × c_page + n × c_tuple
      + n × q × c_op
C_seq = 5,000 × 1.0 + 400,000 × 0.01
      + 400,000 × 2 × 0.0025
C_seq = 5,000 + 4,000 + 2,000
C_seq = 11,000
where
C_seq: the estimated total cost of the sequential scan, in planner cost units
P: the number of pages, 5,000
c_page: `seq_page_cost`, 1.0 per page
n: the number of rows, 400,000
c_tuple: `cpu_tuple_cost`, 0.01 per row processed
q: the number of filter conditions evaluated on each row, 2
c_op: `cpu_operator_cost`, 0.0025 per condition per row
In words: pages cost 5,000, processing rows 4,000 and testing two conditions on every row 2,000.
```

Apply the same model to the illustrative plan: `orders` has 7,353 pages and 1,000,000 rows. With one condition: 7,353 + 10,000 + 2,500 = 19,853. With two: 22,353. These match the illustrative costs in the lesson.

questions.prompt: A `users` table has 2,000,000 rows with distinct lowercase, non-NULL emails, including `ann@example.com`. EXPLAIN for `WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@example.com'` estimates `rows=10000`. Where does 10,000 come from, and what improves it?

options.text: It's 1/200 of the table: the default 0.5% selectivity for equality on an expression without statistics; an expression index on `lower(email)` gives ANALYZE something to measure
options.explanation: Correct. Postgres has stats on `email` but not on `lower(email)`. An expression index makes ANALYZE gather stats on the expression, and also lets the query use the index.

options.text: It's from the histogram for `email`
options.explanation: The histogram describes `email` values, not `lower(email)`. The planner can't see through the function to use them.

options.text: It's 2,000,000 / n_distinct; running ANALYZE will fix it
options.explanation: Emails are unique, so 1/n_distinct would give 1 row. ANALYZE alone doesn't collect stats on arbitrary expressions.

options.text: It's a sign the table needs VACUUM FULL
options.explanation: Table bloat changes page counts and costs, not this selectivity. 10,000 is a fixed default fraction.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
n_est = s_def × n_table
n_est = 0.005 × 2,000,000
n_est = 10,000
where
n_est: the estimated number of matching rows
s_def: the default selectivity for an equality condition with no usable statistics, 0.005 (0.5%), a constant in PostgreSQL's source code
n_table: the number of rows in the table, 2,000,000
In words: with nothing to go on, the planner guesses that half a percent of the rows match.
```

The true answer is 1, so the estimate is 10,000 times too high. That could push the planner away from an index in a join. In the lesson, the same default gave 500 for 100,000 customers. After

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email));
ANALYZE users;
```

the statistics can support an estimate near 1 and make an Index Scan attractive; exact plans depend on the data and cost settings.

lessons.title: Searching the join-order space
lessons.summary: Searching the join-order space with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

The optimiser predicts cardinalities, applies a cost model, and searches candidate plans. Cardinality errors can dominate plan quality: the Leis et al. study in Further reading documents this on its evaluated workloads.

## Searching the plan space

For each table the planner generates the candidate access paths (seq scan, each usable index, bitmap scans). It then has to choose a **join order**, and that space explodes:

| Tables | Left-deep orders | All tree shapes |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 6 | 12 |
| 5 | 120 | 1,680 |
| 10 | 3,628,800 | 17,643,225,600 |

Both columns come from counting arrangements:

```formula
L(n) = n!
T(n) = (2 × n − 2)! / (n − 1)!
L(10) = 10! = 3,628,800
T(10) = 18! / 9! = 17,643,225,600
where
L(n): the number of left-deep join orders for n tables: each step joins one more base table to the result so far, so an order is just a sequence of the tables
T(n): the number of join trees of any shape (left-deep or bushy), counting which input goes on which side of each join
n: the number of tables being joined
!: factorial: multiply all the whole numbers from 1 up to the number, so 3! = 1 × 2 × 3 = 6
In words: the number of possible plans grows faster than exponentially, so trying them all is hopeless beyond a handful of tables.
```

The three-table row follows the same factorial counts: six left-deep orders and twelve ordered, labelled trees. These counts assume unrestricted joins among distinct tables; they exclude physical method choices and illegal reorderings.

Postgres uses System R-style **dynamic programming**. It finds the best way to join every pair of tables, then every set of three built from those, and so on. It keeps the cheapest plan for each subset, plus any plan that produces a useful sort order (an "interesting order") that might avoid a sort later. Working over subsets rather than full orderings is what makes it tractable:

```formula
N_sub = 2^n
N_sub = 2^10 = 1,024
where
N_sub: the number of subsets of the tables, counting the empty set; each table is either in a subset or not, giving 2 choices per table
n: the number of tables being joined, here 10
In words: ten tables have only 1,024 subsets, against 3.6 million orderings.
```

The work per subset still varies, because each subset can be split in several ways and each split has several physical join methods, but the count stays far below the number of trees.

At or above `geqo_threshold` (default 12) FROM items, exhaustive search is too slow, so Postgres switches to **GEQO**, a genetic algorithm that finds a good plan rather than the best. Separately, `join_collapse_limit` (default 8) caps how many explicit `JOIN`s are merged into one list for reordering.

## Key takeaways
- Dynamic programming reuses subset paths and retains useful ordering alternatives.
- Join restrictions, pruning, collapse limits and GEQO constrain search; the cheapest estimated candidate need not run fastest.

## Further reading
- [Statistics used by the planner — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-stats.html)
- [Row estimation examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/row-estimation-examples.html)
- [Multivariate statistics examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/multivariate-statistics-examples.html)
- [Access path selection in a relational DBMS (Selinger et al., 1979)](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/compsci516/cps216/spring03/papers/selinger-etal-1979.pdf)
- [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (Leis et al., VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf)
- [Genetic query optimiser — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/geqo.html)

questions.prompt: A query becomes much slower after a plan change. Which diagnostic checks the cardinality-estimation problem highlighted by the cited optimiser study?

options.text: The cost constants (like `random_page_cost`) are wrong
options.explanation: Cost constants matter, but they rarely change on their own, and studies found they cause far smaller errors than wrong row counts.

options.text: The search strategy missed the best join order
options.explanation: Below the default GEQO threshold, PostgreSQL uses a dynamic-programming search subject to join restrictions and pruning; it does not guarantee the globally fastest real execution plan.

options.text: Compare estimated and actual row counts throughout the plan
options.explanation: Correct. Row estimates feed every cost calculation. A large error, from stale stats or correlated columns, can flip the choice of join algorithm or access path.

options.text: The parser chose a different interpretation of the SQL
options.explanation: With the same input text and parser settings, parsing follows the same grammar. Plan choices can change with statistics, settings and available paths after analysis.

questions.workedExample:
The optimiser has three parts: estimation, cost model, search. Leis et al. (VLDB 2015) tested several real systems and found:

1. Cardinality estimates were often wrong by orders of magnitude, especially after several joins.
2. Those errors, not the cost model, caused most of the slow plans.

So when a plan suddenly changes, compare `rows=` (estimated) with `actual rows=` at each node and look for the first big gap.

link.title: How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (VLDB 2015)

questions.prompt: Which statements about how PostgreSQL searches for a join order are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Below `geqo_threshold` (default 12) FROM items, it uses dynamic programming over subsets of tables
options.explanation: Correct. It builds the best plan for each subset from the best plans of smaller subsets, System R style.

options.text: It tries every possible join tree, which for 10 tables is over 17 billion shapes
options.explanation: There are that many trees, which is exactly why it doesn't enumerate them. Dynamic programming reuses the best plan for each subset (1,024 subsets for 10 tables).

options.text: At or above the threshold (with GEQO enabled) it uses a genetic algorithm (GEQO) that finds a good plan but not necessarily the best
options.explanation: Correct. GEQO trades optimality for planning time on very large joins.

options.text: It may keep a more expensive path for a subset if that path produces a sort order useful later
options.explanation: Correct. These "interesting orders" (pathkeys in Postgres) can avoid a later sort, for a merge join or an ORDER BY.

options.text: Explicit `JOIN` syntax always fixes the join order exactly as written
options.explanation: Explicit inner JOINs can be reordered when flattened. `join_collapse_limit` limits flattening, but exceeding it does not freeze every join inside the retained subtrees. Outer joins also constrain legal reordering.

questions.workedExample:
Count the space for 10 tables:

```formula
L(n) = n!
L(10) = 10! = 3,628,800
T(n) = (2 × n − 2)! / (n − 1)!
T(10) = 18! / 9! ≈ 1.76 × 10^10
N_sub = 2^n = 2^10 = 1,024
where
L(n): the number of left-deep join orders for n tables
T(n): the number of join trees of any shape for n tables
N_sub: the number of subsets of the n tables
n: the number of tables, 10
!: factorial: multiply all whole numbers from 1 up to the number, so 3! = 6
10^10: ten to the power 10; 1.76 × 10^10 is about 17.6 billion
≈: approximately equal to
In words: there are 17.6 billion possible trees but only 1,024 subsets, which is why the planner works over subsets.
```

Dynamic programming avoids that:

1. Best plan for each single table.
2. Best plan for each pair, using step 1.
3. Best for each triple, using step 2. And so on.

The number of subsets doubles with each extra table, but search work also includes candidate partitions and physical paths, so the subset count is not a general time-complexity bound. It also keeps paths with useful sort orders. At 12 or more FROM items, GEQO is used by default to limit search time. `join_collapse_limit = 8` stops explicit JOIN lists longer than 8 being flattened for reordering.

lessons.title: Stale statistics after a load
lessons.summary: Stale statistics after a load with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Stale statistics

Statistics describe the table as it was at the last ANALYZE. Autovacuum re-analyses a table once enough rows have changed since the last ANALYZE:

```formula
n_trig = n_base + k_scale × n_table
n_trig = 50 + 0.1 × 1,000
n_trig = 150
where
n_trig: the number of inserted, updated or deleted rows since the last ANALYZE that defines the analysis threshold; exceeding it makes the table eligible, rather than guaranteeing immediate analysis
n_base: `autovacuum_analyze_threshold`, a fixed number of rows, default 50
k_scale: `autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor`, the fraction of the table, default 0.1 (10%)
n_table: the table's estimated row count (`pg_class.reltuples`, updated by VACUUM and ANALYZE), here 1,000
In words: a table is re-analysed after about a tenth of it has changed, plus 50 rows.
```

For the 1,000-row table below, more than 150 changes cross the threshold, and a 500,000-row load passes that easily. But autovacuum only checks tables periodically (every minute by default, set by `autovacuum_naptime`), so a query run straight after the load still sees the old statistics. On a 100-million-row table, more than 10,000,050 changes cross the default threshold. In between, the planner can be badly wrong:

```sql
-- events: 1,000 rows of kind 'a',
-- analysed. Now load 500,000 of 'b':
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events
WHERE kind = 'b';
```

```
Seq Scan on events  (rows=1)
-- after ANALYZE:
Seq Scan on events  (rows=499881)
```

The planner did notice that the table had grown, because it scales `reltuples` by the current number of pages. But the MCV list said every row is 'a', so 'b' looked almost non-existent. Feed that "1 row" into a join and you get a nested loop running hundreds of thousands of loops, like the 600,000-loop example in the next lesson.

Practical rules:

- Run `ANALYZE` after bulk loads, before querying the new data.
- **Temporary tables are never analysed by autovacuum.** Analyse them yourself.
- For skewed columns, raise the per-column target: `ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 1000;`
- Add extended statistics for correlated columns used together.

## Key takeaways
- ANALYZE after a bulk load avoids relying on old column distributions.
- Temporary tables need manual ANALYZE; autovacuum thresholds make a table eligible rather than scheduling immediate analysis.

## Further reading
- [Statistics used by the planner — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/planner-stats.html)
- [Row estimation examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/row-estimation-examples.html)
- [Multivariate statistics examples — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/multivariate-statistics-examples.html)
- [Access path selection in a relational DBMS (Selinger et al., 1979)](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/compsci516/cps216/spring03/papers/selinger-etal-1979.pdf)
- [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (Leis et al., VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf)
- [Genetic query optimiser — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/geqo.html)

questions.prompt: An ETL job creates a temporary table, inserts 2,000,000 rows (all with `batch = 1`), then immediately runs a join filtered on `WHERE t.batch = 1`. EXPLAIN shows the temp table scan estimated at `rows=10000` (actual 2,000,000), and the plan sorts that "small" input for a merge join. Why is the estimate wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: The planner doesn't know how big the temp table is; use a real table
options.explanation: It does know the size: without a filter, the same scan was estimated at about 2,000,100 rows from the table's page count. What it lacks is column statistics. A real table has the same problem until autovacuum analyses it.

options.text: Autovacuum never analyses temporary tables, so there are no column statistics and `batch = 1` gets the default 0.5% selectivity; run `ANALYZE` on the temp table after loading it
options.explanation: Correct. 0.5% of 2,000,000 is 10,000. Autovacuum can't access temp tables, so they only get stats if you ANALYZE them. With stats, the planner sees that every row matches and picks a hash join.

options.text: `work_mem` is too low; increase it
options.explanation: `work_mem` affects whether a sort or hash spills, not the row estimate. The plan shape came from believing only 10,000 rows match.

options.text: The join needs an index on the temp table
options.explanation: An index won't fix the misestimate. With accurate stats a hash join is right for 2,000,000 rows, and it doesn't need an index.

questions.workedExample:
1. Unfiltered, the scan estimate is about 2,000,100 rows: Postgres measures the table's current pages and estimates rows from them.
2. But `pg_stats` has nothing for `batch`: no ANALYZE has run, and autovacuum skips temp tables (it can't see another session's temporary data).
3. So `batch = 1` gets the default equality selectivity:

```formula
n_est = s_def × n_table
n_est = 0.005 × 2,000,000
n_est = 10,000
where
n_est: the estimated number of matching rows
s_def: the default selectivity for an equality condition with no usable statistics, 0.005 (0.5%), a constant in PostgreSQL's source code
n_table: the number of rows in the table, 2,000,000
In words: with no statistics on `batch`, the planner guesses that half a percent of the rows match.
```

4. The true selectivity is 100%, so the estimate is 200x too low and the join is planned for a small input.
5. Fix:

```sql
INSERT INTO tmp_load ...;
ANALYZE tmp_load;
SELECT ... JOIN orders ...;
```

After ANALYZE, the same query became a hash join estimated at the right size.

questions.prompt:
A staging table was loaded with 600,000 new rows after its last ANALYZE. The join plan shows:

```
Nested Loop (rows=3)
  (actual rows=1800000.00)
-> Seq Scan on imports m
     (rows=1) (actual
     rows=600000.00)
-> Index Scan on order_items
     (actual loops=600000)
Buffers: shared hit=3589400
```

After `ANALYZE`, the planner picks a hash join that touches about 19,000 buffers. What went wrong?

options.text: The index on `order_items` is corrupt
options.explanation: The index worked: it returned 3 rows per lookup, exactly as expected. The problem is how many lookups were made.

options.text: Nested loops are always worse than hash joins
options.explanation: With 99 outer rows the nested loop was the right choice (0.4 ms). The algorithm isn't bad; it was picked for the wrong input size.

options.text: The planner estimated 1 outer row from stale statistics, so a nested loop with one index probe looked cheapest; in reality it made 600,000 probes
options.explanation: Correct. A 1-row estimate makes index nested loop look nearly free. The actual 600,000 loops touched 3.6 million buffers, about 190 times more than the hash join.

options.text: `work_mem` was too small for a hash join
options.explanation: After ANALYZE the hash join ran fine with the same `work_mem`. The planner never considered hashing worthwhile because it believed there was only 1 row.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare estimate with actual on the outer side: `rows=1` vs `600000`. That's a 600,000x misestimate.
2. Cost model with 1 outer row: one index probe, about 16 cost units. Nothing beats that.
3. Reality: 600,000 probes x ~6 buffers each ~ 3.6 million buffer accesses.
4. After ANALYZE: the planner sees 600,000 rows and hashes them instead (~19,000 buffers).

The counts here are illustrative, not audited laptop measurements. Repeated buffer visits are not necessarily distinct disk reads, even on an initially cold cache. The unit on stale statistics explains why the estimate was 1.
