lessons.title: EXPLAIN estimates and execution fields
lessons.summary: EXPLAIN estimates and execution fields with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

`EXPLAIN` is the single most useful tool for understanding a slow query. It shows the plan the optimiser chose, with its estimates. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` also runs the query and shows what actually happened. The skill is reading the output quickly and knowing which numbers matter.

The following abbreviated PostgreSQL 18-style plan fragments are illustrative exercises.

## The variants

```sql
-- plan and estimates only; doesn't run
EXPLAIN SELECT ...;

-- runs it, adds actual rows, time, buffers
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;

-- the options worth knowing
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE,
         SETTINGS, FORMAT JSON) SELECT ...;
```

- **ANALYZE** executes the statement and reports actual figures.
- **BUFFERS** reports pages touched. Since Postgres 18 it's included automatically with ANALYZE; on older versions, ask for it.
- **VERBOSE** adds output column lists and schema-qualified names.
- **SETTINGS** lists any planner settings that differ from the defaults. Very useful when someone sends you a plan.
- **FORMAT JSON** gives machine-readable output for visualisers.
- **TIMING OFF** keeps row counts but skips per-node timing, which can have noticeable overhead on some systems.

> [!warning] EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement
> `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders` deletes the orders. Wrap data-changing statements in a transaction you roll back:
> `BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE ...; ROLLBACK;`
> Rollback does not undo sequence increments or external side effects from functions or triggers. Use disposable data when those effects are possible.

## Anatomy of one node

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending';
```

```
Seq Scan on orders
  (cost=0.00..19853.00 rows=30767 width=26)
  (actual time=0.025..26.566
   rows=30066.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (status = 'pending'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 969934
  Buffers: shared hit=7011 read=342
Planning Time: 0.133 ms
Execution Time: 27.149 ms
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cost=0.00..19853.00` | Estimated startup..total cost, in planner units |
| `rows=30767` | Estimated rows output |
| `width=26` | Estimated average row size in bytes |
| `actual time=0.025..26.566` | Real ms to first row..last row |
| `rows=30066.00` | Real rows output, per loop |
| `loops=1` | Times this node was executed |
| `Rows Removed by Filter` | Rows read but rejected |
| `Buffers: shared hit` | Pages found in Postgres's cache |
| `Buffers: shared read` | Pages fetched from the OS or disk |

From this one node: the estimate (30,767) was within about 2.3% of the truth (30,066), the scan read every one of the 7,353 pages (7,011 + 342), and it threw away 97% of the rows it read. The last fact is the important one. Reading a million rows to keep 30,000 is a sign that an index might help (see the index-tuning units).

The `.00` on actual rows is new in Postgres 18. It's there because `rows` is an **average per loop**, and averages needn't be whole numbers, as you'll see below.

## Key takeaways
- Plain EXPLAIN shows estimates; ANALYZE executes the statement, including mutations.
- PostgreSQL 18 includes BUFFERS with ANALYZE and displays fractional average actual rows and index search counts.

## Further reading
- [Using EXPLAIN — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/using-explain.html)
- [EXPLAIN command reference — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-explain.html)
- [auto_explain — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/auto-explain.html)
- [pg_stat_statements — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstatstatements.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18.html)
- [EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN — SQLite docs](https://www.sqlite.org/eqp.html)

questions.prompt: A colleague wants to see why a cleanup statement is slow and runs `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE ordered_on < '2021-01-01';` on production. What happens?

options.text: Nothing is deleted; EXPLAIN never modifies data
options.explanation: Plain EXPLAIN doesn't, but `ANALYZE` makes it actually execute the statement in order to measure it.

options.text: The rows are really deleted, and the plan with actual timings is shown
options.explanation: Correct. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement for real. To undo transactional changes after measuring, wrap it: `BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE ...; ROLLBACK;`. Sequence advances and external trigger effects are not necessarily undone.

options.text: Postgres refuses: EXPLAIN ANALYZE only works on SELECT
options.explanation: It works on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE and more. That's what makes it both useful and dangerous.

options.text: The rows are deleted but automatically restored after the EXPLAIN finishes
options.explanation: There's no automatic rollback. Outside an explicit transaction, the change is committed as normal.

questions.prompt:
A node reads:

```
Seq Scan on customers
  (cost=0.00..2529.00 rows=500
   width=49)
  (actual time=0.109..16.982
   rows=1.00 loops=1)
```

Which statement is right?

options.text: The scan returned 500 rows and took 2,529 ms
options.explanation: 500 is the planner's estimate and 2,529 is an estimated cost in planner units. Neither is a measurement.

options.text: The planner estimated 500 rows; the scan actually returned 1 row and finished after about 17 ms
options.explanation: Correct. The first parentheses are estimates; the `actual` ones are measurements. A 500x overestimate is worth investigating.

options.text: The scan returned 1 row 500 times
options.explanation: `loops=1`, so the node ran once. `rows=500` in the first group is an estimate, not a loop count.

options.text: The rows are 49 KB wide on average
options.explanation: `width` is in bytes: about 49 bytes per row.

questions.workedExample:
Split the node into its two groups:

| Group | Figures |
|---|---|
| Estimate | cost 0..2529, 500 rows, 49 B wide |
| Actual | 0.109 ms to first row, 16.982 ms to last, 1 row, 1 loop |

This came from `WHERE lower(email) = '...'`. The 500 is the default 0.5% guess for an expression without statistics (0.005 x 100,000).

questions.prompt: Which statements about EXPLAIN output in **PostgreSQL 18** are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` includes buffer counts without needing the BUFFERS option
options.explanation: Correct. Postgres 18 made BUFFERS the default when ANALYZE is used.

options.text: Actual row counts are shown with decimals, such as `rows=2.50`, because they are averages per loop
options.explanation: Correct. Earlier versions rounded the per-loop average to an integer, which could hide fractional averages (e.g. 0.4 rows per loop shown as 0).

options.text: Index scans report `Index Searches`, the number of index descents, which skip scan can make larger than the number of loops
options.explanation: Correct. In the lesson, a skip scan made 1,031 descents in one loop.

options.text: Costs are now shown in milliseconds
options.explanation: Costs are still in planner units anchored on `seq_page_cost = 1.0`. Only `actual time` is in milliseconds.

options.text: Plain `EXPLAIN` (without ANALYZE) also shows actual row counts
options.explanation: Without ANALYZE the query isn't executed, so there's nothing actual to report. Only estimates are shown.

questions.workedExample:
Postgres 18 changed EXPLAIN in several visible ways:

1. `ANALYZE` implies `BUFFERS`. True.
2. Fractional actual rows: `rows=10.01 loops=12500` shows on average just over 10 rows per lookup. True.
3. `Index Searches: N` per index node. True.
4. Costs remain unitless planner estimates. False.
5. Plain EXPLAIN does not report actual row counts. The option claiming it does is false. Planning can still evaluate immutable expressions, so do not treat EXPLAIN as a sandbox for arbitrary functions.

lessons.title: Inclusive time, loops and row errors
lessons.summary: Inclusive time, loops and row errors with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Three rules for the numbers

### 1. Costs and times are cumulative

A node's cost and time **include its children's**. To find the time spent in one node itself (its *exclusive* time), subtract its children. From the illustrative cities query:

```
Hash Join  (actual time=12.237..44.658)
-> Seq Scan on orders o
     (actual time=0.013..25.815)
-> Hash  (actual time=12.038..12.038)
```

```formula
t_excl = t_node − Σ t_child
t_excl = (44.658 − 25.815 − 12.038) ms
t_excl ≈ 6.8 ms
where
t_excl: the node's exclusive time: the time spent in the node itself, in milliseconds (ms)
t_node: the node's inclusive time, the second number of its `actual time`, here 44.658 ms for the Hash Join
t_child: a child's inclusive time, the second number of its `actual time`: 25.815 ms for the orders scan and 12.038 ms for the Hash
Σ: sum: add up the term for every child
≈: approximately equal to
ms: millisecond, a thousandth of a second
In words: of the 44.7 ms reported for the Hash Join, about 6.8 ms was spent joining; the rest was its children.
```

For serial totals, multiply both the parent's and each child's average time by their own `loops` before subtracting; the displayed example has one loop at every node. With parallel execution, loops may include executions by several processes. Multiplying averages by loops gives aggregate instrumented execution time, not elapsed wall-clock time; overlapping worker times cannot simply be subtracted from the leader time. Worker details, rescans and instrumentation overhead make exclusive-time subtraction only a diagnostic approximation.

So most of the 47 ms went on the orders scan (26 ms), not the join.

### 2. Multiply by loops

`actual time` and `rows` are **per loop**. The inner side of a nested loop runs once per outer row:

```
Nested Loop  (actual rows=600.00 loops=1)
-> Index Only Scan using orders_pkey
     (actual rows=200.00 loops=1)
-> Index Scan using order_items_order_id_idx
     (actual time=0.000..0.001
      rows=3.00 loops=200)
     Index Searches: 200
     Buffers: shared hit=1191 read=9
```

```formula
n_total = n_loop × L
n_total = 3.00 × 200 = 600
t_total ≈ t_loop × L
t_total ≈ 0.001 ms × 200 = 0.2 ms
where
n_total: the total number of rows the node produced across all its executions
n_loop: the `rows` figure: the average number of rows per execution, here 3.00
L: the `loops` figure: the number of times the node was executed, here 200 (once per outer row)
t_total: the total time spent in the node across all executions, in milliseconds (ms)
t_loop: the per-execution time, the second number of `actual time`, here 0.001 ms
≈: approximately equal to (the per-loop time is a rounded average)
ms: millisecond, a thousandth of a second
In words: 200 lookups of 3 rows each is 600 rows, and 200 lookups of about a microsecond each is about 0.2 ms.
```

`Buffers` are already **totals** across all loops, not per loop: 1,200 page accesses, 6 per lookup.

### 3. Compare estimated rows with actual rows

This is the most important check. Walk up from the leaves and find the **lowest node where the estimate and the actual differ by 10x or more**. Everything above it was planned on wrong information.

```
Nested Loop  (rows=3)
  (actual rows=1800000.00)
-> Seq Scan on imports m  (rows=1)
     (actual rows=600000.00)
     Filter: (batch = 2)
-> Index Scan using order_items_order_id_idx
     (rows=3) (actual rows=3.00
      loops=600000)
Buffers: shared hit=3589400
```

The Seq Scan on `imports` expected 1 row and got 600,000. When both counts are positive, measure the gap as a ratio, whichever way round is bigger. A zero estimate or zero actual count needs direct inspection instead of division:

```formula
r = max(n_act / n_est, n_est / n_act)
r = max(600,000 / 1, 1 / 600,000)
r = 600,000
where
r: the misestimate factor: how many times too high or too low the estimate was; 1 means exact
n_act: the actual rows per loop, from `actual rows`, here 600,000
n_est: the estimated rows, the `rows` figure in the first brackets, here 1
max: the larger of the two values
In words: the estimate was 600,000 times too low, far beyond the 10x that marks a serious error.
```

That's the root cause. The nested loop above it was a reasonable choice for 1 row and a poor one for 600,000: 3.6 million page accesses. After `ANALYZE imports`, the planner chose a hash join with about 19,000.

> [!tip] Estimates the other way are dangerous too
> An overestimate can make the planner reject an index and scan a whole table. Any big gap is worth explaining.

## Key takeaways
- Rows and time are averages per loop; buffers are totals.
- Serial inclusive-time subtraction is approximate; parallel worker time can overlap. Investigate estimate errors from the leaves upwards.

## Further reading
- [Using EXPLAIN — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/using-explain.html)
- [EXPLAIN command reference — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-explain.html)
- [auto_explain — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/auto-explain.html)
- [pg_stat_statements — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstatstatements.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18.html)
- [EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN — SQLite docs](https://www.sqlite.org/eqp.html)

questions.prompt:
```
Hash Join  (actual time=31.0..80.0
            rows=50000.00 loops=1)
-> Seq Scan on a
     (actual time=0.01..50.0 loops=1)
-> Hash  (actual time=20.0..20.0
          loops=1)
```

How much time was spent in the Hash Join node itself (its exclusive time)?

options.text: 80 ms
options.explanation: 80 ms is the inclusive time: it covers the children too. Times in EXPLAIN ANALYZE are cumulative.

options.text: 49 ms
options.explanation: That's 80 - 31, the gap between first and last row. Part of that is the scan of `a` streaming rows in.

options.text: 30 ms
options.explanation: That only subtracts the Seq Scan. The Hash child's 20 ms is also included in the join's 80 ms.

options.text: About 10 ms
options.explanation: Correct. 80 ms total, minus 50 ms in the probe-side scan, minus 20 ms building the hash, leaves about 10 ms for probing and joining.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
t_excl = t_node − Σ t_child
t_excl = (80.0 − 50.0 − 20.0) ms
t_excl = 10.0 ms
where
t_excl: the exclusive time: time spent in the Hash Join itself, in milliseconds (ms)
t_node: the node's inclusive time, the second number of its `actual time`, 80.0 ms
t_child: a child's inclusive time: 50.0 ms for the scan of a, 20.0 ms for the Hash
Σ: sum: add up the term for every child
ms: millisecond, a thousandth of a second
In words: subtract the children's durations from the node's total, and 10 ms is left for probing and joining.
```

Both children ran once, so no loop multiplication is needed. The real bottleneck is the scan of `a` (50 ms), so that's where to look first: is it reading far more rows than it returns?

questions.prompt:
The inner side of a nested loop shows:

```
Index Scan using items_order_idx
  (actual time=0.010..0.012
   rows=2.50 loops=4000)
```

How many rows did this node return in total, and roughly how long did it take altogether?

options.text: 10,000 rows in about 48 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Figures are per loop: 2.5 rows x 4,000 loops = 10,000 rows, and 0.012 ms x 4,000 = 48 ms.

options.text: 2.5 rows in 0.012 ms
options.explanation: Those are per-loop averages. The node ran 4,000 times.

options.text: 4,000 rows in 0.012 ms
options.explanation: 4,000 is the number of executions, not rows; and the time must be multiplied by loops too.

options.text: It can't return half a row, so the plan is corrupt
options.explanation: 2.50 is an average over 4,000 loops: some lookups found 2 rows, others 3. Postgres 18 prints the decimals for exactly this reason.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
n_total = n_loop × L
n_total = 2.50 × 4,000 = 10,000
t_total ≈ t_loop × L
t_total ≈ 0.012 ms × 4,000 = 48 ms
where
n_total: the total rows the node returned across all executions
n_loop: the `rows` figure, the average rows per execution, 2.50
L: the `loops` figure, the number of executions, 4,000
t_total: the total time spent in the node, in milliseconds (ms)
t_loop: the per-execution time to the last row, the second number of `actual time`, 0.012 ms
≈: approximately equal to
ms: millisecond, a thousandth of a second
In words: 4,000 lookups of 2.5 rows each is 10,000 rows, and 4,000 lookups of 0.012 ms is 48 ms.
```

A 0.012 ms node looks harmless until you multiply it by its loops. That's how a nested loop with a very cheap inner side can still dominate a query.

questions.prompt:
Which node is the most likely **root cause** of this bad plan?

```
Hash Join (rows=484)
  (actual rows=3686.00)
-> Seq Scan on orders o
     (rows=30767)
     (actual rows=30066.00)
-> Hash (rows=1573)
     (actual rows=12500.00)
   -> Seq Scan on customers c
        (rows=1573)
        (actual rows=12500.00)
        Filter: city = 'Glasgow'
          AND country = 'Scotland'
```

options.text: The Hash Join, because its estimate (484) is furthest from the actual (3,686)
options.explanation: The join's error is inherited: it multiplies its inputs' estimates. Fix the input and the join estimate improves.

options.text: The Seq Scan on `orders`, because it reads the most rows
options.explanation: Its estimate (30,767) is within 3% of the actual (30,066). Big isn't the same as wrong.

options.text: There's no problem; the estimates are all close
options.explanation: The customers estimate is 8x too low and the join is 7.6x too low. That's enough to change plan choices in a bigger query.

options.text: The Seq Scan on `customers`, where correlated city and country conditions are underestimated by 8x
options.explanation: Correct. It's the lowest node with a big error. The planner multiplied 1/8 x 1/8 as if the columns were independent, but city determines country.

questions.workedExample:
Walk up from the leaves:

| Node | Est | Actual | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scan orders | 30,767 | 30,066 | 1.0x |
| Scan customers | 1,573 | 12,500 | 8x |
| Hash Join | 484 | 3,686 | 7.6x |

The first big error is on `customers`, and the join inherits it. Fix: `CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies) ON city, country`, then ANALYZE.

lessons.title: Spills and index access conditions
lessons.summary: Spills and index access conditions with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Red flags and what they indicate

| You see | It suggests |
|---|---|
| Estimate off by 10x+ | Stale stats, correlated columns, or a function on a column |
| Large `Rows Removed by Filter` | A missing or unusable index |
| `Sort Method: external merge  Disk:` | Sort spilled; `work_mem` too small, or an index could supply the order |
| `Batches:` greater than 1 | Hash spilled to temp files |
| High `loops` on an expensive inner node | Nested loop over too many outer rows |
| `Heap Fetches` high on an Index Only Scan | Pages are not all-visible; investigate updates, snapshots and vacuum |
| `Heap Blocks: lossy` | Bitmap too big for `work_mem`; rows rechecked per page |
| `Buffers: ... read` dominates | Absent from shared buffers; the OS cache may still serve reads |

### Sorts that spill

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY total;
```

```
Sort  (actual time=238.774..288.495
       rows=1000000.00 loops=1)
  Sort Key: total
  Sort Method: external merge
    Disk: 36344kB
  Buffers: temp read=9084 written=9101
```

With the default 4 MB `work_mem`, sorting a million rows wrote 36 MB to temporary files. Interestingly, `work_mem = 64MB` *still* spilled: the in-memory quicksort needed 71 MB (`Memory: 71451kB` at 256 MB), because in-memory sorting carries per-row overhead the compact on-disk format doesn't. With an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` instead, the plan uses `top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB` and never spills.

### Index Cond versus Filter

```
Index Scan using customers_email_pattern_idx
  Index Cond: ((email ~>=~ 'c42@'::text)
    AND (email ~<~ 'c42A'::text))
  Filter: (email ~~ 'c42@%'::text)
```

**Index Cond** is evaluated by the index access method. Leading-key bounds usually narrow a B-tree search; some later-key conditions filter index entries without reducing the contiguous range scanned. **Filter** is checked on each row after it's fetched. A condition appearing only under Filter does not supply an index access condition in that node. Here the `LIKE 'c42@%'` prefix was converted into a range for the index, then rechecked as a filter.

### New in Postgres 18: Index Searches

```
Index Scan Backward
  using orders_date_cust_idx
  Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
  Index Searches: 1031
```

`Index Searches` counts how many separate descents into the index happened. Normally it's 1 per loop. Here, an index on `(ordered_on, customer_id)` was used for a query on `customer_id` alone, and Postgres 18's **skip scan** made 1,031 descents, across the date groups it checked. The composite-index unit explains how a leading customer key can need one search.

## Key takeaways
- Spills, high loops and heap fetches are evidence to investigate, rather than proof of one fix.
- Index Cond is handled by the index method; a separate Filter is evaluated after that access.

lessons.title: Buffers and a slow-query investigation
lessons.summary: Buffers and a slow-query investigation with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Reading BUFFERS

Each buffer is one page, normally 8 KiB, so the counts convert to volumes. For `Buffers: shared hit=7011 read=342`:

```formula
V = n_buf × 8 KiB
V_hit = 7,011 × 8 KiB = 56,088 KiB
V_hit ≈ 54.8 MiB
V_read = 342 × 8 KiB = 2,736 KiB
V_read ≈ 2.7 MiB
where
V: the volume of data the buffer accesses represent
n_buf: the number of buffer (page) accesses in the count
V_hit: the volume served from Postgres's shared memory
V_read: the volume requested from the operating system
KiB: kibibyte, 1,024 bytes
MiB: mebibyte, 1,024 KiB
≈: approximately equal to
In words: about 55 MiB came from Postgres's own cache and under 3 MiB had to be requested from the operating system.
```

Repeated accesses to the same page count again each time, so this is a measure of work, not of distinct data.

- **hit**: already in shared buffers.
- **read**: requested from the operating system. It might still have come from the OS page cache, so a `read` is not necessarily a disk read. Enable `track_io_timing` to measure time spent in I/O calls. It still cannot tell whether those calls were served from the OS cache or physical storage.
- **dirtied / written**: pages this query modified or had to write out (for example, setting hint bits on freshly loaded rows).
- **temp read / written**: temporary files from spilling sorts and hashes.

Buffer access counts complement timing, but they are not independent of system state. The hit/read split depends on cache warmth, and repeated accesses may revisit the same page. The illustrative totals (3.6 million versus 19,000) suggest very different work, but do not imply that every access becomes a separate disk read on a cold cache.

## A method for slow queries

1. Get the real plan: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` against production-sized data. A plan from a 1,000-row dev table tells you little.
2. Note the total `Execution Time`.
3. Find the nodes with the largest **exclusive** time (subtract children, multiply by loops).
4. Walk up from the leaves looking for the first big estimate error.
5. Check the red flags table.
6. Change one thing (an index, ANALYZE, a rewrite), then re-run and compare buffers and time.

For long plans, paste the text into a visualiser such as [explain.depesz.com](https://explain.depesz.com/) or [explain.dalibo.com](https://explain.dalibo.com/), which compute exclusive times and highlight misestimates for you.

To catch slow plans in production without running EXPLAIN by hand, use the **auto_explain** module, which logs the plans of statements slower than a threshold, and **pg_stat_statements**, which records total time and calls for each query shape (queries that differ only in their constant values are counted together) so you know which queries to look at first.

> [!note] Other databases
> MySQL has `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (8.0.18+) with a similar tree format. SQLite's `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is much terser:
> `SCAN o`, then `SEARCH c USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)`, then `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY`. That was our cities query: a nested loop of primary-key lookups, with a temporary B-tree for the grouping.

## Caveats

- EXPLAIN ANALYZE doesn't send the result rows to the client, so network transfer time isn't included. Postgres 17 added a `SERIALIZE` option to measure the cost of converting rows to output format.
- Repeated runs change cache warmth. Compare multiple representative runs and inspect `read` versus `hit`; two runs do not establish production behaviour.
- Per-node timing has overhead. If the plan has millions of tiny loops, use `TIMING OFF` and rely on row counts and buffers.

## Key takeaways
- Buffer counters describe accesses, including repeated visits; shared reads can hit the OS cache.
- Compare representative plans and timings, including client costs omitted by EXPLAIN.

## Further reading
- [Using EXPLAIN — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/using-explain.html)
- [EXPLAIN command reference — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-explain.html)
- [auto_explain — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/auto-explain.html)
- [pg_stat_statements — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstatstatements.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18.html)
- [EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN — SQLite docs](https://www.sqlite.org/eqp.html)

options.text: `shared hit` counts pages found in Postgres's shared buffer cache
options.explanation: Correct. Hits are served from Postgres's own memory without asking the operating system.

options.text: `shared read` always means the page came from disk
options.explanation: Not necessarily. A read means Postgres asked the OS, and the OS may have it in its page cache. Turn on `track_io_timing` to see actual I/O time.

options.text: `temp read` and `temp written` come from sorts or hashes that spilled
options.explanation: Correct. Temp buffers are temporary-file traffic, typically from `work_mem` being too small for a sort or hash.

options.text: With the usual 8 KiB block size, `hit=12800` represents 100 MiB of buffer accesses, possibly revisiting pages
options.explanation: Correct. 12,800 × 8 KiB = 100 MiB of accesses; this is not necessarily 100 MiB of distinct data.

options.text: A node's buffer counts are per loop, so multiply by `loops`
options.explanation: Buffer counts are totals across all loops, unlike `rows` and `actual time`, which are per-loop averages.

questions.workedExample:
1. hit = Postgres shared buffers. True.
2. read = from the OS, which could be its cache or the disk. False as stated.
3. temp = spill files. True.
4. At the usual block size, 12,800 accesses of 8 KiB each represent 100 MiB of accesses, not necessarily distinct data. True.
5. In the lesson, an inner index scan with `loops=200` showed `Buffers: shared hit=1191 read=9`: 1,200 in total, i.e. 6 per lookup. That's a total, not a per-loop figure. False.

questions.prompt: You test two plans for a batch join on a warm-cache test server. Plan A (nested loop) took 575 ms with `Buffers: shared hit=3589400 read=13260`. Plan B (hash join) took 527 ms with about 19,000 buffers and some temp I/O. Production has far less RAM than the working set. Which plan should you expect to hold up better in production, and why?

options.text: Plan A, because it was nearly as fast and uses no temp files
options.explanation: Nearly all its 3.6 million accesses were shared-buffer hits, with 13,260 reads that might still hit the OS cache. With a cold or small cache, many become random disk reads.

options.text: They are equivalent because their times are within 10%
options.explanation: Times measured on a warm cache hide I/O cost. The work done differs by about 190x.

options.text: Plan B is a promising candidate because it makes far fewer buffer accesses; validate with representative cache and I/O conditions
options.explanation: Correct. Total buffer accesses help measure work, but the hit/read split depends on cache state and accesses may revisit the same page. Plan B reads each table once in order; Plan A does 600,000 index descents.

options.text: Neither: you can only decide by running them both in production
options.explanation: Measuring in production is ideal, but buffer counts guide investigation but do not guarantee performance across machines and cache states.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
B_A = 3,589,400 + 13,260 = 3,602,660
r = B_A / B_B
r ≈ 3,602,660 / 19,000 ≈ 190
where
B_A: Plan A's buffer accesses: shared hits plus shared reads
B_B: Plan B's buffer accesses, about 19,000
r: how many times more page accesses Plan A makes
≈: approximately equal to
In words: Plan A touches pages about 190 times as often as Plan B.
```

On the staging box nearly all of A's accesses were hits, so they avoided OS read requests; their individual latency was not measured. Suppose instead some became random SSD reads:

```formula
t_extra ≈ f × B_A × t_read
t_extra ≈ 0.1 × 3,602,660 × 0.1 ms
t_extra ≈ 36,000 ms = 36 s
where
t_extra: the extra time if that fraction of Plan A's accesses became real reads
f: the fraction of accesses assumed to miss every cache, here 0.1 (10%)
B_A: Plan A's buffer accesses, 3,602,660
t_read: the assumed time for one random SSD read, about 0.1 ms
ms: millisecond, a thousandth of a second
s: second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: if one access in ten went to the SSD, Plan A would gain about 36 seconds.
```

This is a hypothetical calculation, not a measured hardware prediction. Compare buffer accesses and measured timings under representative conditions.

lessons.title: Selectivity means pages as well as rows
lessons.summary: Selectivity means pages as well as rows with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

The System Design module's indexing lesson covers how B-trees and LSM trees work. This lesson takes the planner's point of view: given a query and its plan, which index would change the plan, and is the change worth what the index costs?

The examples below assume an illustrative 1,000,000-row `orders` table and PostgreSQL 18 plan features.

## Will the planner use the index?

An index lets Postgres jump to matching entries, but each match still needs its row fetched from the table (the **heap**). If the rows are scattered, each fetch can be a different page. The planner compares that random I/O with simply reading the whole table in order.

Three queries on `ordered_on` with an index on that column:

| Filter | Rows | Plan | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| One day | 438 | Bitmap index scan | 0.5 ms |
| One quarter | 37,390 (3.7%) | Bitmap index scan | 9.3 ms |
| Since 2021 | 847,258 (85%) | Seq Scan | 51 ms |

The quarter is the interesting one. A sequential scan took 23 ms, so the index halved the time, but look at the plan:

```
Bitmap Heap Scan on orders
  (actual rows=37390.00)
  Heap Blocks: exact=7306
-> Bitmap Index Scan on orders_date_idx
```

Matching 3.7% of the rows touched 7,306 of 7,353 heap pages, nearly all of them. Orders for a given quarter are spread uniformly through the table (physical-order correlation near 0), so almost every 8 KiB page contains a few. You can predict that: if matching rows are scattered at random, the chance that a page has none at all is tiny.

```formula
m = r_page × s
m = 136 × 0.037 ≈ 5
p_none = (1 − s)^{r_page}
p_none = 0.963^{136} ≈ 0.006
P_hit ≈ P × (1 − p_none)
P_hit ≈ 7,353 × 0.994 ≈ 7,309
where
m: the average number of matching rows on each heap page
r_page: the number of rows on each heap page, about 136 for `orders`
s: the selectivity: the fraction of rows that match, here 0.037 (3.7%) for one quarter
p_none: the probability that a page holds no matching row, if each row matches independently at random; one factor of (1 − s) per row on the page, all multiplied together
P: the number of heap pages in the table, 7,353
P_hit: the expected number of heap pages holding at least one matching row
≈: approximately equal to
In words: with about 5 matches per page on average, only about 1 page in 170 escapes, so the index scan still visits about 99.4% of the pages.
```

The prediction, about 7,309 pages, is close to the 7,306 the plan reported. The model assumes matches are scattered at random; any clustering by date lowers the page count. A bitmap scan visits matching heap pages in physical order. Whether it beats a sequential scan when nearly every page is touched must be measured; the illustrative timing is not a general guarantee. But the benefit of an index depends on **how many pages** the matching rows occupy, not just how many rows match.

If rows were physically clustered by this date column (for example, an append-only log written in date order), the same quarter would occupy about 4% of the pages, and the index would win by far more.

> [!note] Bitmap scans
> A **Bitmap Index Scan** collects the locations of all matches into an in-memory bitmap of pages; the **Bitmap Heap Scan** then reads those pages in physical order. It's the planner's middle ground between an index scan (good for a few rows) and a seq scan (good for many). Bitmaps from different indexes can be combined with `BitmapAnd` and `BitmapOr`.

## Key takeaways
- Scattered matches can touch most pages even at low row selectivity.
- Bitmap scans gather tuple locations and visit heap pages in physical order; compare their cost with a full scan.

## Further reading
- [Multicolumn indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-multicolumn.html)
- [Index-only scans and covering indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-index-only-scans.html)
- [Partial indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-partial.html)
- [Combining multiple indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-bitmap-scans.html)
- [Operator classes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-opclass.html)
- [Use The Index, Luke: SQL indexing for developers](https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
- [Heap-only tuples (HOT) — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/storage-hot.html)

questions.prompt: There is an index on `orders(ordered_on)`, but `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ordered_on >= '2021-01-01'` uses a Seq Scan. The filter matches 847,258 of 1,000,000 rows. Why?

options.text: The index is corrupt and needs REINDEX
options.explanation: The same index was used for narrower date ranges. The planner simply chose not to use it for this one.

options.text: Postgres can't use B-tree indexes for `>=`
options.explanation: B-trees support range comparisons; the index served a one-quarter range in the same lesson.

options.text: Statistics are stale
options.explanation: The estimate was 846,113 rows against 847,258 actual, which is very accurate. The planner estimated the matching count closely.

options.text: With 85% of rows matching, reading the whole table sequentially is cheaper than an index walk plus heap fetches
options.explanation: Correct. An index would read most of the index and then nearly every heap page anyway, at higher cost per page. The seq scan reads 7,353 pages once, in order.

questions.workedExample:
1. Matching rows: 85%.
2. An index scan would read ~85% of the index entries and fetch rows from virtually every heap page (each page holds ~136 rows).
3. A seq scan reads every page once, sequentially, at `seq_page_cost = 1` instead of `random_page_cost = 4`.

For this illustrative wide-row range query, the estimated sequential scan is cheaper. Indexes can also help broad queries by supplying order or covering their output columns.

questions.prompt: Each heap page holds about 136 rows, and the rows matching a filter are spread randomly through the table. The filter matches 3.7% of rows. Roughly what fraction of pages contain at least one matching row?

options.text: About 3.7%
options.explanation: That would be true only if matching rows were clustered together on the same pages, i.e. high correlation. Randomly spread, they land on most pages.

options.text: About 37%
options.explanation: That's off by a factor of ten in the wrong direction. With 136 rows per page, a typical page holds about 5 matches.

options.text: About 50%
options.explanation: There's no reason for a half. Compute the probability that a page has no matches: 0.963 to the power 136.

options.text: About 99%
options.explanation: Correct. The chance that a page has no match is 136 copies of 0.963 multiplied together, about 0.006, so about 99.4% of pages have at least one. For illustration, 7,306 of 7,353 pages would be about 99.4%.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
p_miss = 1 − s = 1 − 0.037 = 0.963
p_none = p_miss^{r_page} = 0.963^{136}
p_none = e^{136 × ln(0.963)}
p_none = e^{−5.13} ≈ 0.006
p_hit = 1 − p_none ≈ 0.994
where
p_miss: the probability that one row does not match
s: the selectivity: the fraction of rows matching, 0.037
p_none: the probability that none of a page's rows match, assuming each row matches independently at random
r_page: the number of rows per page, 136
e: Euler's number, about 2.718, the base of natural logarithms
ln: the natural logarithm (logarithm to base e); ln(0.963) ≈ −0.0377
p_hit: the probability that a page holds at least one match, which is the fraction of pages the scan visits
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a page escapes only if all 136 of its rows miss, and that happens to only about 1 page in 170.
```

Each page has on average 136 × 0.037 ≈ 5 matches. This is why `correlation` matters so much to the cost of an index scan: with data clustered by the filtered column, the same 3.7% of rows would occupy about 3.7% of the pages.

lessons.title: Composite indexes and skip scan
lessons.summary: Composite indexes and skip scan with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Composite indexes: column order is everything

A frequent query: a customer's five most recent orders.

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY ordered_on DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

With an index on `(customer_id, ordered_on)`:

```
Limit  (actual rows=5.00)
-> Index Scan Backward using
     orders_cust_date_idx on orders
     Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
     Index Searches: 1
     Buffers: shared hit=5 read=3
Execution Time: 0.032 ms
```

The index holds customer 42's entries side by side, already sorted by date. Postgres descends once, walks backwards and stops after five. There's no Sort node at all.

Now the same columns the other way round, `(ordered_on, customer_id)`:

```
Limit  (actual rows=5.00)
-> Index Scan Backward using
     orders_date_cust_idx on orders
     Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
     Index Searches: 1031
     Buffers: shared hit=2067 read=1047
Execution Time: 3.084 ms
```

Customer 42's entries are now scattered across every date. Postgres 18's **skip scan** rescues the query by making repeated searches across date groups (1,031 illustrative searches before finding five matches). That's about 100 times slower and 390 times more buffers than the right index. Earlier PostgreSQL versions could still use the index and check the later-key condition, but without skip scan might need to read a much larger index range. Other indexes and restrictions could change the choice.

> [!tip] Order the columns: equality, then sort, then range
> 1. Columns compared with `=` go first.
> 2. Then the `ORDER BY` column, so rows come out in order.
> 3. Then columns compared with ranges (`<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`).
>
> Equality on leading keys and a range on the next key establish the usual scan bounds. Later conditions can still be checked within the index, and PostgreSQL 18 skip scan may perform additional searches to narrow work further. Check the actual plan rather than treating the rule as absolute.

Skip scan is usually most attractive when the omitted leading key has relatively few distinct values. PostgreSQL 18 chooses repeated searches only when its cost model expects an advantage; the exact search count need not equal the global distinct-value count, especially with LIMIT or additional bounds. With 2,400 dates it gave 2,400 descents for a full lookup (6.4 ms). With a million distinct leading values it would be hopeless. Design for the query; don't rely on skip scan.

## Key takeaways
- Leading equality keys followed by the desired ordering can let LIMIT stop an ordered scan early.
- PostgreSQL 18 skip scan can use repeated searches, but its usefulness depends on omitted-key distinctness and other bounds.

The "recent orders" widget runs this query thousands of times a minute:

```sql
WHERE customer_id = $1
ORDER BY ordered_on DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Which single index serves it best?

options.text: `(ordered_on, customer_id)`
options.explanation: With the date first, one customer's entries are scattered across every date. The illustrative example uses 1,031 index descents via skip scan and was about 100x slower.

options.text: `(customer_id, ordered_on)`

options.text: Separate indexes on `customer_id` and on `ordered_on`

options.text: `(ordered_on)` alone

2. Sort: `ordered_on DESC` -> second column (a B-tree can be read backwards).

```
-> Index Scan Backward using
     orders_cust_date_idx
     Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
```

questions.prompt: A dashboard runs `WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND ordered_on >= now() - interval '7 days'`. Which composite index puts these conditions into a single contiguous B-tree range, without relying on skip scan?

options.text: `(ordered_on, status)`
options.explanation: With the range column first, the scan reads every order of the last week and checks `status` entry by entry. Without skip scan, status does not reduce the initial contiguous date range. PostgreSQL 18 may use skip scan to avoid some irrelevant entries.

options.text: Either order is identical; B-trees treat columns symmetrically
options.explanation: A B-tree sorts by the first column, then the second within ties. The order decides which conditions bound the scan.

options.text: `(status, ordered_on)`
options.explanation: Correct. Equality first: all cancelled orders are together, sorted by date, so the scan starts at the first cancelled order from 7 days ago and stops at the last. Both conditions bound it.

options.text: `(status)` alone
options.explanation: That finds all ~70,000 cancelled orders and checks each date. The date range doesn't narrow the scan.

questions.workedExample:
Picture the sorted index entries:

```
(status, ordered_on):
 cancelled 2020-01-01
 ...
 cancelled 2026-07-20  <- start
 cancelled 2026-07-27  <- stop
 pending   2020-01-01
 ...
```

On Postgres 18, with only an index on `(ordered_on, customer_id)`, `WHERE customer_id = 42` shows:

```
  Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
```

options.text: Postgres read the whole table 2,400 times

lessons.title: Covering and partial indexes
lessons.summary: Covering and partial indexes with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Covering indexes and index-only scans

If every column a query needs is in the index, Postgres can answer from the index alone: an **Index Only Scan**. `INCLUDE` adds columns to the index's leaf entries without making them part of the key:

```sql
-- Store payload needed by this report.
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_cov_idx
  ON orders (customer_id)
  INCLUDE (ordered_on, total);

SELECT customer_id, ordered_on, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 1 AND 2000;
```

There's a catch. The index doesn't record whether each row version is visible to your transaction, so Postgres must check the table **unless** the page is marked all-visible in the **visibility map**. VACUUM can set those bits; unchanged all-visible pages then permit the heap check to be skipped. Here is the query (20,162 rows) straight after updating 2% of the table, and again after a VACUUM:

| State | Heap Fetches | Buffers | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Just after updating 20,000 rows | 20,592 | 20,661 | 27.6 ms |
| After VACUUM | 0 | 81 | 1.1 ms |

The 20,000 updated rows were spread across nearly every page, so nearly every page lost its all-visible bit. The "index-only" scan went back to the heap for every row and became 25 times slower. Index-only scans work best on tables that are mostly read, or where autovacuum keeps up.

## Partial indexes

If queries only ever look at a small subset of rows, index only that subset:

```sql
-- Keep only pending entries in the index.
CREATE INDEX orders_pending_idx
  ON orders (ordered_on)
  WHERE status = 'pending';
```

```
Limit  (actual rows=20.00)
-> Index Scan using orders_pending_idx
Execution Time: 0.049 ms
```

The partial index holds 30,066 entries and is 272 kB. The full index on `ordered_on` is 6.9 MB. It's cheaper to maintain too: a shipped-order insert adds no entry to it.

The planner uses a partial index only when it can **prove** the query's WHERE clause implies the index's predicate. `WHERE status = 'pending'` matches. `WHERE status = $1` with a parameter usually doesn't, because the planner can't prove `$1` is 'pending' when building a generic plan.

## Key takeaways
- Covering columns enable index-only access only when visibility checks can avoid heap fetches.
- A partial index is usable only when the planner can establish its predicate; a generic unknown parameter can prevent that proof.

## Further reading
- [Multicolumn indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-multicolumn.html)
- [Index-only scans and covering indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-index-only-scans.html)
- [Partial indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-partial.html)
- [Combining multiple indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-bitmap-scans.html)
- [Operator classes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-opclass.html)
- [Use The Index, Luke: SQL indexing for developers](https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
- [Heap-only tuples (HOT) — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/storage-hot.html)

questions.prompt: A reporting query uses a covering index and normally shows `Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 0` in about 1 ms. Right after a nightly job updates 2% of the table, the same plan shows `Heap Fetches: 20592` and takes 27 ms. What's going on?

options.text: The index became bloated and needs REINDEX
options.explanation: Bloat would make the index bigger, but it doesn't explain heap fetches. Those come from visibility checks.

options.text: The updates cleared all-visible bits in the visibility map, so Postgres must check the heap for row visibility until VACUUM runs
options.explanation: Correct. An index-only scan skips the heap only for pages marked all-visible. The scattered updates touched nearly every page, so nearly every row needed a heap check. After VACUUM it was back to 0 heap fetches and 1.1 ms.

options.text: The planner switched to a different plan
options.explanation: It's the same Index Only Scan. The node type didn't change; the amount of heap work did.

options.text: The INCLUDE columns were dropped from the index
options.explanation: Updates don't change an index's definition. If columns were missing, it couldn't be an index-only scan at all.

questions.workedExample:
1. Index entries don't record transaction visibility; the heap does.
2. The visibility map has a bit per heap page: "every row here is visible to everyone".
3. An UPDATE writes a new row version and clears that bit for the page.
4. 20,000 updated rows over 7,353 pages (~136 rows each) clears the bit on nearly every page.
5. So the index-only scan fetches the heap for almost every row: 20,592 heap fetches, 20,661 buffers.
6. VACUUM can set all-visible bits when every relevant row version is visible to all transactions; long-running snapshots can delay this.

Fix: let autovacuum run sooner on that table, or run `VACUUM` straight after the nightly job.

questions.prompt: Given `CREATE INDEX orders_pending_idx ON orders (ordered_on) WHERE status = 'pending';`, which queries are eligible to use it, assuming suitable surrounding SELECT statements? Select all that apply.

options.text: `WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY ordered_on LIMIT 20`
options.explanation: Correct. The WHERE matches the index predicate, and the index supplies `ordered_on` order. An illustrative runtime is 0.049 ms.

options.text: `WHERE status = 'pending' AND ordered_on < '2021-01-01'`
options.explanation: Correct. The predicate is implied, and the date range is an index condition on the key column.

options.text: `WHERE ordered_on < '2021-01-01'` (any status)
options.explanation: No. The index only contains pending orders, so using it would miss shipped and cancelled ones.

options.text: `WHERE status IN ('pending', 'cancelled')`
options.explanation: No. The query asks for cancelled orders too, which aren't in the index.

options.text: A prepared statement `WHERE status = $1` executed with a generic plan
options.explanation: No. With a generic plan, the planner can't prove `$1` equals 'pending', so it can't assume every row the query needs is in the index.

questions.workedExample:
The test is: does the query's WHERE clause *logically imply* `status = 'pending'`?

| Query condition | Implies it? |
|---|---|
| status = 'pending' AND ... | Yes |
| ordered_on < ... only | No |
| status IN (pending, cancelled) | No |
| status = $1 (generic) | Can't prove |

Only when it's implied can the planner be sure every row the query needs is in the index.

lessons.summary: Expressions, patterns and bitmap combinations with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## Expression indexes and operator classes

An index on `email` does not directly search the lower-case expression in `WHERE lower(email) = ...`, because the index stores `email`, not `lower(email)`. Index the expression:

```sql
-- Store lower-case values as search keys.
CREATE INDEX customers_lower_email_idx
  ON customers (lower(email));
```

| Index | Plan | Time |
|---|---|---|
| None | Seq Scan, 99,999 removed | 17 ms |
| On `lower(email)` | Index Scan | 0.02 ms |

For the simple equality shown, an ordinary email index cannot supply a selective lower-case-expression lookup. It can still be scanned as a covering path in some queries; a function does not make every use of an index impossible.

ANALYZE also gathers statistics on indexed expressions, so the row estimate improves from the 0.5% default (500) to 1.

Pattern planning also depends on the collation and operator. These examples assume a deterministic collation; PostgreSQL 18 supports LIKE with some nondeterministic collations, but index support still needs checking for the specific expression and pattern.

**Operator classes** matter for `LIKE`. In a database whose collation isn't `C`, a plain B-tree on a text column can't serve `LIKE 'abc%'`, because the collation's sort order doesn't keep prefixes together byte-wise. An index built with `text_pattern_ops` can:

```sql
-- Use byte-order keys for LIKE prefixes.
CREATE INDEX customers_email_pattern_idx
  ON customers (email text_pattern_ops);
```

A pattern beginning with a wildcard such as `LIKE '%abc'` supplies no selective prefix range for an ordinary B-tree. A full or index-only scan can still use that index as a covering access path. For indexed substring search, consider a trigram index (`pg_trgm` with GIN or GiST).

## Combining indexes

Postgres can combine single-column indexes with bitmaps:

```
Bitmap Heap Scan on orders
  (actual rows=308.00)
-> BitmapAnd
   -> Bitmap Index Scan
        on orders_cust_cov_idx
        Index Cond: (customer_id < 500)
        (actual rows=4984.00)
   -> Bitmap Index Scan on orders_date_idx
        Index Cond:
          (ordered_on < '2020-06-01')
        (actual rows=63535.00)
Execution Time: 2.148 ms
```

It read 4,984 and 63,535 index entries to find 308 rows. A suitable composite index may reduce the work for this exact query, but bitmap combination means a few well-chosen single-column indexes can serve many query shapes reasonably. That's often the better trade when queries are ad hoc.

## Key takeaways
- Match an expression index to the expression searched, and check collation and operator-class requirements for prefixes.
- Bitmap combinations can serve varied predicates but do not preserve B-tree ordering.

- [Index-only scans and covering indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-index-only-scans.html)
- [Partial indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-partial.html)
- [Combining multiple indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-bitmap-scans.html)
- [Operator classes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-opclass.html)
- [Use The Index, Luke: SQL indexing for developers](https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
- [Heap-only tuples (HOT) — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/storage-hot.html)

questions.prompt: `customers` has a B-tree index on `email`. The login query is `WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)` and EXPLAIN shows a Seq Scan. What's the right fix?

options.text: Create an index on the expression: `CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email))`
options.explanation: Correct. The index then stores `lower(email)` values, so the condition matches it exactly. In the illustrative comparison the lookup goes from 17 ms to 0.02 ms.

options.text: Run ANALYZE so the planner notices the existing index
options.explanation: The planner already knows the index exists. It lacks a selective lower-case search bound because the index stores `email`, not `lower(email)`. A full covering scan remains possible in a different plan.

options.text: Add `/*+ INDEX(email) */` as a hint
options.explanation: Core Postgres has no optimiser hints, and no hint can make an index of `email` answer a question about `lower(email)`.

options.text: Make the index UNIQUE
options.explanation: Uniqueness doesn't change which expression is indexed, so it still can't be used.

questions.workedExample:
For a selective search using this equality condition, the indexed expression must match (or have a supported equivalent):

| Indexed | Query uses | Usable? |
|---|---|---|
| `email` | `email = ...` | Yes |
| `email` | `lower(email) = ...` | No |
| `lower(email)` | `lower(email) = ...` | Yes |

Bonus: ANALYZE then collects statistics on `lower(email)`, so the estimate changes from the 0.5% default (500 rows) to 1.

questions.prompt: Your database uses the `en_US.UTF-8` collation. A plain B-tree index on `customers(email)` isn't used for `WHERE email LIKE 'c42@%'`. What will let an index serve this query?

options.text: Nothing; B-trees can never serve LIKE
options.explanation: B-trees can serve prefix LIKE patterns when the operator class compares byte-wise (the `C` collation or `text_pattern_ops`).

options.text: A B-tree index with the `text_pattern_ops` operator class
options.explanation: Correct. It orders values byte by byte, so a prefix becomes a range (`>= 'c42@'` and `< 'c42A'`). This supports the illustrated Index Cond; actual runtime must be measured.

options.text: A hash index on `email`
options.explanation: Hash indexes support only equality. They have no notion of prefixes or ranges.

options.text: Rewriting the pattern as `LIKE '%c42@%'`
options.explanation: A leading wildcard supplies no useful prefix range for an ordinary B-tree, though a covering index can still be scanned. A pg_trgm GIN or GiST index can support selective substring searches.

questions.workedExample:
1. Locale collations like `en_US` sort with linguistic rules (case and punctuation handled specially), so strings sharing a byte prefix aren't guaranteed to be contiguous in the index.
2. `text_pattern_ops` sorts by raw bytes, so all strings starting `c42@` are contiguous.
3. Postgres turns the LIKE into a range:

```
Index Cond:
  ((email ~>=~ 'c42@'::text)
   AND (email ~<~ 'c42A'::text))
Filter: (email ~~ 'c42@%'::text)
```

(`A` is the byte after `@`.) It then rechecks the LIKE as a filter.

lessons.summary: Index maintenance and tuning a workload with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

## What every index costs

| Index | Size |
|---|---|
| orders (the table) | 59 MB |
| orders_cust_cov_idx | 30 MB |
| orders_pkey | 21 MB |
| orders_cust_date_idx | 21 MB |
| orders_date_idx | 6.9 MB |
| orders_pending_idx | 272 kB |

The illustrative date index is smaller in part because of **B-tree deduplication** (Postgres 13+), which stores a repeated key once with a list of row pointers: 1,000,000 rows share only 2,400 distinct dates.

Costs to weigh:

- **Writes.** An INSERT maintains applicable indexes; a partial index excludes rows outside its predicate. Changing a column used by a non-summarising index, including an `INCLUDE` column, prevents a **HOT** (heap-only tuple) update. BRIN is a summarising-index exception; HOT also requires room on the original heap page.
- **Memory.** Indexes compete with table data for the buffer cache.
- **Vacuum.** Vacuum may need index cleanup for dead tuples; its actual work depends on dead-index entries and cleanup settings, and unnecessary scans can be skipped.
- **Planning.** More indexes give more paths to consider, and more chances of a surprising choice.

Find indexes that are never used:

```sql
-- Zero scans is a lead, not drop approval.
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan,
  pg_size_pretty(
    pg_relation_size(indexrelid))
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0;
```

Check over weeks of traffic, and on replicas, before dropping anything. Also look for **redundant** indexes: an index on `(customer_id)` is usually redundant next to one on `(customer_id, ordered_on)`, which serves the same lookups.

## A tuning workflow

1. Find the queries that matter with `pg_stat_statements`, ordered by `total_exec_time` (the execution durations of every call added together, so a fast query called a million times can outrank a slow one called once), not just the slowest single run.
2. Get `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on production-sized data.
3. Design an index for the query: equality columns, then sort, then range; add `INCLUDE` columns only if an index-only scan is worth the size.
4. To permit ordinary writes during the build, use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. It takes additional work, can wait for transactions, and cannot run in a transaction block. A failure can leave an INVALID index that still adds maintenance overhead; inspect and clean up or rebuild it.
5. Re-run EXPLAIN and compare buffers and time. Watch write latency afterwards.

## Key takeaways
- INCLUDE columns consume space and can prevent HOT updates when they change.
- Review usage over a representative window, replicas and constraints before treating an index as redundant.

- [Index-only scans and covering indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-index-only-scans.html)
- [Partial indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-partial.html)
- [Combining multiple indexes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-bitmap-scans.html)
- [Operator classes — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-opclass.html)
- [Use The Index, Luke: SQL indexing for developers](https://use-the-index-luke.com/)
- [Heap-only tuples (HOT) — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/storage-hot.html)

questions.prompt: `orders.total` is updated frequently as items are added. To make a report index-only, someone changes the index on `customer_id` to `(customer_id) INCLUDE (ordered_on, total)`. Write latency on `orders` rises noticeably. What's the most likely mechanism?

options.text: INCLUDE columns are sorted, so every update re-sorts the index
options.explanation: INCLUDE columns aren't part of the key and aren't sorted. That's what distinguishes them from key columns.

options.text: The index is now larger than the table, so writes go to disk
options.explanation: The covering index (30 MB) is still smaller than the table (59 MB). Size alone isn't the main mechanism here.

options.text: Updates to `total` can no longer use HOT because this B-tree INCLUDE column changed, increasing index maintenance
options.explanation: Correct for the ordinary B-tree indexes in this example. Changing an INCLUDE column prevents HOT and requires index maintenance. In general, BRIN summarising indexes are an exception, and partial indexes only hold matching rows.

options.text: The planner now uses the index for the UPDATE's WHERE clause, which is slower
options.explanation: The excerpt concerns increased index-maintenance work. A plan used to locate UPDATE targets can also affect runtime, so inspect both aspects rather than assuming an index always makes target lookup faster.

questions.workedExample:
How a HOT update works:

1. If no indexed column changes and the page has free space, the new row version goes on the same page, chained from the old one.
2. Indexes still point to the old version and follow the chain. No index writes.

Once `total` is in an index (even as INCLUDE), changing it means:

1. Not HOT-eligible.
2. New entries in applicable ordinary indexes, plus more WAL; partial indexes omit nonmatching rows and summarising indexes such as BRIN behave differently.

Check `n_tup_hot_upd` vs `n_tup_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables` before and after. Only cover columns that rarely change.

questions.prompt: You're auditing the indexes on a busy table. Which of these statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An index on `(customer_id)` is usually redundant if there's also one on `(customer_id, ordered_on)`
options.explanation: Correct. The composite index serves any lookup on `customer_id` alone, because it's the leading column. The single-column one adds write cost for little gain (it may be slightly smaller and faster to scan).

options.text: `idx_scan = 0` in `pg_stat_user_indexes` on the primary proves an index is safe to drop
options.explanation: Not on its own. Statistics are per server, so replicas may use it. It may serve a monthly job, or enforce a UNIQUE constraint without ever being scanned.

options.text: If `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` fails, it can leave an INVALID index that can still add write overhead and needs cleanup or rebuilding
options.explanation: Correct. Depending on the failure stage, an INVALID index may still be maintained on writes while being ignored for queries. Drop it and retry, or recreate it with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.

options.text: Adding more indexes always makes reads faster and has no effect on reads that don't use them
options.explanation: Indexes compete for cache memory and add planning work. Writes slow down too, which can hurt reads through locks and I/O contention.

options.text: A B-tree on a low-cardinality column can be much smaller than one on a unique column, thanks to B-tree deduplication
options.explanation: Correct. Since Postgres 13, duplicates are stored once with a list of row pointers. In the lesson the date index (2,400 values) was 6.9 MB against 21 MB for the unique primary key.

questions.workedExample:
1. Leftmost prefix: `(customer_id, ordered_on)` answers `customer_id = ?`. True.
2. Index usage stats are per instance and reset on stats reset; unique indexes enforce constraints without scans. False.
3. Concurrent builds can fail on deadlocks or uniqueness violations and leave `INVALID` indexes. True.
4. Indexes cost cache, planning and write time. False.
5. B-tree deduplication shrinks indexes with many repeated keys. True.

**Content gap — benchmark evidence:** plan and timing figures here are illustrative scenarios, not independently reproduced measurements. The original dataset and run record are unavailable; actual timings, memory use and plan choices require testing on a representative system.

lessons.title: Functions, casts and search predicates
lessons.summary: Functions, casts and search predicates with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: `customers(id, name, email, city, country)`, `orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total)`, `products(id, price)` and `order_items(order_id)`. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use `date`, IDs use `integer`, and totals use `numeric`. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context.

All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are **illustrative inputs**, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown.

Most slow queries aren't exotic. They are a handful of recurring shapes that stop the planner using an index, make it misestimate, or make it do work the application didn't need. Each section below shows the anti-pattern, an illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style plan, and the fix.

The indexes on `orders` at this point are the primary key, `(customer_id, ordered_on)`, `(customer_id) INCLUDE (ordered_on, total)`, `(ordered_on)` and the partial index on pending orders.

## 1. Functions on indexed columns

```sql
-- Year extraction is a column expression.
SELECT count(*) FROM orders
WHERE extract(year FROM ordered_on) = 2025;
```

```
Seq Scan on orders  (rows=5000)
  (actual rows=152653.00)
  Filter: (EXTRACT(year FROM ordered_on)
           = '2025'::numeric)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 847347
Execution Time: 65.983 ms
```

Two things went wrong. The index on `ordered_on` cannot provide a selective search bound for this expression, because it is sorted by `ordered_on`, not by `extract(year ...)`. And the estimate is the default 0.5% (5,000) instead of 152,653, because there are no statistics on the expression. Rewrite the condition as a range on the bare column:

```sql
-- Half-open bounds retain the whole year.
WHERE ordered_on >= '2025-01-01'
  AND ordered_on <  '2026-01-01'
```

```
Index Only Scan using orders_date_idx
  (actual rows=152653.00)
  Heap Fetches: 0
Execution Time: 8.652 ms
```

That's 7.6 times faster, with an accurate estimate. A condition the database can answer with an index is called **sargable** (from "search argument"). The same trap catches `date(created_at) = ...`, `lower(email) = ...`, `col + 1 = 10` and `coalesce(col, 0) = 5`. Either rewrite it so the bare column is compared, or create an expression index that matches it.

## 2. Type mismatches

```sql
-- Inspect a numeric cast on integer IDs.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE id = 42.0;
```

```
Seq Scan on orders  (rows=5000)
  Filter: ((id)::numeric = 42.0)
```

`id` is an integer and `42.0` is numeric, so Postgres converts every `id` to numeric to compare them. That removes the selective search bound on the ordinary integer primary-key index; a different query might still scan the index as a covering path. `WHERE id = '42'` is fine, because an untyped literal is converted to the column's type.

This usually comes from application code: a driver that sends a parameter as numeric or text, or a comparison that casts the indexed column to an incompatible representation. PostgreSQL can support indexed cross-type integer/bigint comparisons; integer/text comparisons may instead need an explicit cast or fail operator resolution. Look for `::` casts on the **column** side of a Filter.

## 3. Leading wildcards

```sql
-- A suffix supplies no B-tree prefix.
WHERE email LIKE '%42@example.com'
```

There is no selective prefix bound for an ordinary B-tree: matches could start with anything, so they are scattered across the whole index. The plan is a Seq Scan reading all 100,000 customers. A prefix (`LIKE 'c42@%'`) can use a `text_pattern_ops` index, as in the previous lesson. For substring search, consider a trigram index (`CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm` plus a GIN or GiST index). Full-text search instead matches processed words or tokens, so it is a different search behaviour.

## Key takeaways
- A half-open range of dates can search an ordinary date index while preserving the intended day or year.
- A cast on an integer column to numeric can remove a useful index bound; supported cross-type comparisons behave differently.

## Further reading
- [Sargable — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargable)
- [Use The Index, Luke: functions in WHERE clauses](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/functions)
- [Use The Index, Luke: paging through results without OFFSET](https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)
- [Don't Do This — PostgreSQL wiki](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This)
- [Subquery expressions (EXISTS, IN, NOT IN) — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-subquery.html)
- [PREPARE and plan_cache_mode — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-prepare.html)
- [Slow counting — PostgreSQL wiki](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Slow_Counting)
- [WITH queries (CTEs) — PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/queries-with.html)

questions.prompt: `events.created_at` is a `timestamp` with a B-tree index. Which rewrite of `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-03-01'` lets the index be used?

options.text: `WHERE created_at::date = '2026-03-01'`
options.explanation: That's the same function in different syntax: a cast applied to the column. The ordinary index on `created_at` still lacks a selective search bound for that expression.

options.text: `WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-02'`
options.explanation: Correct. The bare column is compared with constants, so the condition becomes an index range scan over exactly one day. A half-open range also avoids missing times like 23:59:59.5.

options.text: `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-01'`
options.explanation: It's sargable, but it's wrong: it only matches the instant 2026-03-01 00:00:00, not the whole day.

options.text: `WHERE to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD') = '2026-03-01'`
options.explanation: This formats each column value as text; the ordinary timestamp index supplies no selective bound for that expression. It is a different indexed expression.

questions.workedExample:
An index on `created_at` is sorted by `created_at`. It can find a contiguous range of values, but it knows nothing about `date(created_at)`.

1. Ask: which raw values does the condition accept? All timestamps from midnight on 1 March up to, not including, midnight on 2 March.
2. Write that as a half-open range on the bare column.

In the lesson, the same rewrite for a whole year went from a 66 ms Seq Scan to an 8.7 ms Index Only Scan.
